sens: Percussion instrument made of two metal plates that are struck together
Object used to produce a loud noise in rituals and religious celebrations
H4700.detail:
1. The cymbal is a musical instrument consisting of two bronze or metal plates that the musician strikes against each other to produce a loud and resonant sound. It is a percussion instrument that creates an intense and powerful noise, very different from the strings of the harp or the lute (1 Chronicles 13:8).
2. In the worship of Israel, the cymbal fulfills a liturgical function: it accompanies songs and dances during major celebrations, notably the dedication of the temple and solemn festivals. The bronze cymbals are entrusted to the Levitical musicians-singers, who make them "resound" within the service of the sanctuary to glorify God (1 Chronicles 15:19; 2 Chronicles 5:12).
H4700.origine: The Hebrew word מְצִלְתַּיִם (metsiltayim) is the plural of a form that evokes the loud and metallic sound. It designates the instrument by the nature of the noise it produces: a resounding clap. The word belongs to the family of musical instruments of Israelite worship, alongside the harp and the lute.
H4700.emploi: The word appears thirteen times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in Chronicles and the books of the Exile (Ezra, Nehemiah). It always refers to bronze cymbals used in the temple or during religious festivals. The cymbals are mentioned at solemn moments: the dance before the ark (1 Chronicles 13:8), the organization of worship by David (1 Chronicles 15:19; 25:1), the dedication of the temple (2 Chronicles 5:12), and the rebuilding after the exile (Ezra 3:10; Nehemiah 12:27). They always symbolize the joyful and organized worship of the people of Israel.
H4700.portee: The cymbal reminds the Christian that the worship of God engages everything we have: voice, body, instruments, noise, and joy. It shows that celebration is never silent or amorphous, but loud, visible, and communal. The resounding sound of the cymbal invites the believer to proclaim their praise without fear or restraint.

sens: Official headdress of the high priest in the worship of Israel
Band or turban wrapped around the head
Insignia of dignity and sacred consecration
Royal or princely headdress (figuratively)
H4701.detail:
1. The tiara is the official headdress worn by the high priest during service at the tabernacle and the temple. Made of fine linen, it is an essential element of his sacred garment, alongside the breastplate and the ephod. In Exodus 28:4, it is listed among the garments that the sons of Aaron must wear "so that they may serve as my priests," showing that it marks religious authority.
2. Materially, the tiara is a band or turban wrapped around the head, made of twisted fine linen (Exodus 39:28). It can receive other ornaments: the diadem of holiness is placed on it (Exodus 29:6), and the gold plate engraved with the words "Holiness to the Lord" is attached to it by a blue cord (Exodus 28:37, 39:31).
3. The tiara symbolizes consecration to God and the holiness of the high priest. Wearing it during the performance of priestly duties reminds that the one who wears it is set apart for the service of the Lord and responsible for interceding for the people.
4. In prophetic passages like Ezekiel 21:31, the tiara also represents royal power and dignity, suggesting that certain official headdresses carry this same meaning beyond the priestly context.
H4701.origine: The Hebrew word מִצְנֶפֶת (mitsneféth) specifically designates the turban or tiara. Its etymology refers to the idea of wrapping or binding the head. This type of headdress was common in the ancient Near East as a mark of rank and authority. The biblical context emphasizes its religious and sacred value, particularly in the chapters dedicated to the investiture of the high priest.
H4701.emploi: The word tiara appears 9 times in the Bible, primarily concentrated in the chapters of Exodus dedicated to priestly garments (Exodus 28-29 and 39), where it is described in detail: its material (fine linen), its ornamentation (diadem, gold plate), and its placement on the head of the high priest. It is also found in Leviticus 8:9 during the actual investiture of Aaron, showing that it is not merely a prescription, but a garment actually worn. The passage in Ezekiel 21:31 uses the term in a context of the overturning of dignities, where God commands the removal of tiaras and crowns. In every occurrence, the tiara is associated with an official and sacred function.
H4701.portee: The tiara reminds the reader that the service of God requires visible consecration and personal separation. It illustrates that true religion is not a private matter: it is expressed through concrete and public signs. For the Christian, this image of the high priest adorned with his tiara foreshadows Jesus Christ, our eternal high priest, enthroned in heaven with his glory and honor.

sens: Furniture or surface on which one lies down to sleep or rest
Image of a refuge or inadequate shelter in the face of danger
H4702.detail:
1. The bed is the furniture on which one lies down to sleep or rest the body. It is a place of intimacy and rest. In Isaiah 28:20, the prophet speaks of a bed too short to stretch out on: the image is of a man trying to sleep on an uncomfortable bed, where he cannot lie down fully.
2. The word takes on a figurative meaning when it designates an inadequate refuge or protection. In the same verse, the covering (comforter or sheet) is too narrow to wrap around the body: it is the image of an inadequate defense against misfortune. Isaiah uses it to show that human plans will not protect them from God's judgment.
H4702.origine: The Hebrew word מַצָּע (matzaʿ) comes from a root that evokes the idea of stretching out or lying down. It designates the bed as the place where the body stretches out for rest. It is a simple and concrete term, referring to a piece of furniture from daily life.
H4702.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (in Isaiah 28:20). In this context, the prophet Isaiah criticizes the leaders of Judah who seek human alliances and political strategies to protect themselves from divine judgment. He compares them to someone trying to sleep on a bed too short and a covering too narrow: no human arrangement will be sufficient to save them. The image of the bed expresses inadequacy and insufficiency.
H4702.portee: This image of the bed too short teaches us that our efforts to create security without God are in vain. It reminds us that only God can offer us true rest and real protection. It is an invitation not to seek our salvation in carnal alliances or human strategies, but to rest in God.

sens: succession of steps, walk
progression, advancement in a path or project
entourage, group of people accompanying someone
H4703.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a succession of steps or a walk: each step taken while walking. In Psalms 37:23, "the steps of a man" literally refers to the steps he takes on the path.
2. By extension, it signifies progression or advancement: the manner in which one moves through life, how one pursues their path. In Proverbs 20:24, "the steps of a man" express how his walk (his life) is guided by the Lord.
3. It can also refer to a sequence, an entourage — the group of people who follow or accompany an important figure. In Daniel 11:43, the Libyans and the Ethiopians enter into the "entourage" of the king, meaning they become his companions or subjects in his retinue of power.
H4703.origine: The Hebrew word מִצְעָד comes from the root צעד which evokes the idea of walking, treading, taking steps. It is a concrete word, related to the movement of the body. The same root produces words for "step" and "walk" throughout the Hebrew Bible.
H4703.emploi: This word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the sense of "steps" or "sequence." In Psalms 37:23 and Proverbs 20:24, it refers to the steps of a man — the path he follows, his moral and existential progression. These two passages establish a theology: it is the steps of the righteous that the Lord affirms, and it is He who directs the steps of the wise. In Daniel 11:43, the word takes on a political nuance: the "entourage" of the king, those who are at his disposal, who follow him in his expansion of power. The meaning thus varies between personal walk (moral) and social accompaniment (entourage).
H4703.portee: This word teaches that every step of our life, every progress, is observed and guided by God. It reminds us that our path is not left to chance, but is affirmed by the hand of the Lord when we trust Him. For the believer, this offers assurance: our steps matter, they are known to God, and He orders them.

sens: Of reduced dimensions, quantity, or importance
Short-lived
Having few members or units
H4705.detail:
1. The word describes something of reduced size or volume, or of little importance: the city of Zoar is "small" in its physical dimension (Genesis 19:20), and Job's former prosperity seems "small" compared to what awaits him (Job 8:7).
2. It can qualify a brief duration: Israel possessed the land for only a "short" time (Isaiah 63:18), meaning a short period.
3. The word also applies to a small group: the Syrian army arrived with only a "small number" of men (2 Chronicles 24:24), which makes the victory that God gave to Joash even more remarkable.
H4705.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root expressing the idea of shrinking, diminishing. It describes what is reduced in extent, quantity, or duration. It is a simple and concrete adjective, without any particular pejorative connotation: the small is not contemptible, it is simply of lesser dimension.
H4705.emploi: The word appears four times in the Bible, primarily to describe material or temporal realities. In Genesis 19:20, Lot asks for refuge in a small city; in 2 Chronicles 24:24, a small army becomes the instrument of divine justice; in Job 8:7, Bildad contrasts the former prosperity with what is to come; in Isaiah 63:18, Israel experienced a brief possession of the land. In all cases, the word designates a reduced or minor reality, often in contrast to something larger or more significant.
H4705.portee: This smallness, far from being a weakness, can become the place where God acts: a small army wins the victory, a small number of faithful will inherit the promises. The Christian reader understands that external dimensions do not measure God's power or the value of what He accomplishes. Smallness also invites trust: one is saved only in the small refuge that God offers.

sens: Mountain in Transjordan, in the northern region near Mount Hermon
H4706.detail: Mitsear is a mountain located in Transjordan (the region east of the Jordan), presumably in the north, not far from Mount Hermon. It appears only once in the Bible, in Psalm 42:7, where the psalmist, downcast and far from God, remembers Him "from the land of the Jordan, from Hermon, from the mountain of Mitsear." This mention evokes a precise geographical context, likely a place of exile or pilgrimage, where the believer in distress invokes the memory of divine worship.
H4706.origine: The name Mitsear literally means "small" in Hebrew (from the root צער, tsaar). It designates a secondary mountain, perhaps less famous than the neighboring Hermon, but notable enough to be mentioned alongside this orographic giant. The name simply reflects the relative importance of the peak in the mountainous landscape of Lebanon-Anti-Lebanon.
H4706.emploi: Mitsear appears only once in the Old Testament, in Psalm 42:7. The context is that of a song of distress: the psalmist, chased or exiled, enumerates three famous places in the north of the Holy Land (the Jordan, Hermon, Mitsear) as spiritual landmarks he longs for. This geographical enumeration enhances the emotion of the psalm by recalling the high places of worship and the presence of God.
H4706.portee: This verse reminds us that even in the midst of distress and exile, the believer can invoke the memory of holy places and the past presence of God. The mountains of Mitsear and Hermon become witnesses of divine faithfulness, inviting the reader to cling to the memory of God when all seems lost.

sens: High place from which to observe the territory
Strategic point located at height to observe the enemy or the landscape
Place of surveillance and vigilance
H4707.detail:
1. A high place, either natural or constructed, from which one can survey a wide territory. In 2 Chronicles 20:24, when Judah reaches the "height" from which they can "see" the desert, they can look far and see the enemy's corpses: it is a strategic viewpoint over the landscape.
2. A tower or guard position established for surveillance, particularly to detect a military threat. Isaiah 21:8 speaks of a watchman who cries, "I stand on the tower all day long": it is a fixed position to maintain watch and observe approaching enemies.
3. More broadly, a place of vigilance where the one stationed must remain attentive: the word evokes the tension of one who spies the horizon, day and night, to announce what is coming.
H4707.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to look" or "to see" (צפה, tsafah). The watchtower is thus the place from which "one sees," from which one observes. In the Old Testament, this root appears in several words related to vision or surveillance: it is the basic verb for "to observe" or "to spy." The word מִצְפֶּה itself is formed with the place prefix (מִ-) followed by the root, making it literally "the place where one sees" or "the place of visibility."
H4707.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In 2 Chronicles 20:24, it is a geographical point: a high place in the desert from which Judah can observe from afar. In Isaiah 21:8, it is a military or prophetic post: a position that the watchman occupies to watch and proclaim. Both usages converge on the idea of a place of surveillance, but one is rather a natural place in the landscape, while the other is an established guard post. The warrior or prophetic context prevails: one watches to see the threat or the message coming.
H4707.portee: This word reminds the reader of the importance of vigilance and attention before God. The one placed in a watch position cannot relax: they must remain awake, scanning the horizon. It is a biblical image of faith: the believer is called to watch, to remain attentive to the signs of God in the world and in their life. The watchman of Isaiah 21:8 is also a figure of the prophet who cries the alarm or proclaims the message: it invites us to hear and convey what God wants us to see.

sens: City in the region of Judah
H4708G.detail: Mitspé is a city mentioned in the list of cities in the district of the Shephelah, the lowland region of Judah. Its Hebrew name literally means "watch" or "watchtower," suggesting that it was built in a location that allowed for surveillance of the surrounding territory.
H4708G.origine: The word הִצְפֶּה (mits-peh) comes from the root צפה (tsafah), which means "to watch," "to keep watch," "to observe." This root evokes the image of a person placed high up to observe and warn of dangers. The name of the city thus reflects its probable function: a lookout post or a tower overlooking the region.
H4708G.emploi: Mitspé appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:38, where it is listed among the cities of the territory allocated to the tribe of Judah. It is classified in the Shephelah, the region of low hills between the Mediterranean coast and the heights of Judah. Its single mention suggests that it was a small settlement, likely fortified, serving as a point of observation or defense.

sens: City of Moab, east of the Jordan
H4708H.detail: Mitspé is a city located in the land of Moab, on the other side of the Jordan. Its name means "watchtower" in Hebrew, evoking a fortified place where one watches the surroundings. It is where David took refuge with his parents when he fled from the anger of King Saul (1 Samuel 22:3).
H4708H.origine: The name Mitspé comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to observe, to watch" — hence the idea of a tower or lookout post. Several places bear this name in Israel, but this one is distinguished by its location in Moab. The name recalls the function of such a place: a high point to watch over the territory.
H4708H.emploi: Mitspé appears only once in the Bible at this specific occurrence, in 1 Samuel 22:3, where David brings his parents for safety while he flees Saul. It is a strategic refuge, out of the reach of the king of Israel, in a foreign region but less hostile than the desert.

sens: City of the tribe of Benjamin
H4708I.detail: Mitspé is a city located in the territory of Benjamin, listed among the cities that Joshua distributed to this tribe after the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 18:26).
H4708I.origine: The name comes from the Hebrew mitspaH which means "watchtower" or "observatory" — the place from which one surveys the horizon. This name reflects the defensive function of the place, hence its strategic importance.
H4708I.emploi: Mitspé appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in the list of cities of Benjamin. It is also known by the similar name of Mizpah (mitspaH, pronounced differently), which designates other important sites in the Old Testament. These places bear the same name because it is a generic term for a site of observation or surveillance.

sens: Valley near Mount Hermon, in northern Israel
H4708J.detail: 1. The name Mitspa literally means "watchtower" or "place of observation," as it designates a high place from which one could survey the horizon. This valley was located in northern Israel, in the region of Mount Hermon, which overlooked the entire surrounding territory. In Joshua 11:8, it marks the northern limit of Israel's pursuit after the military victory against the Canaanite kings: the Israelite armies pursued the enemy "as far as the valley of Mitspa to the east," indicating that this place served as a well-known geographical landmark.
H4708J.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to look" or "to spy" (צפה). Mitspa thus literally means "the lookout point" or "watchtower." The same Hebrew name has designated other places in Israel, including a famous city in Benjamin where Samuel and Saul met. Here, Mitspa is a northern location, distinct from these other Mitspa.
H4708J.emploi: Mitspa appears only once in the Bible as a valley: in Joshua 11:8, during the great northern campaign where Joshua pursued the coalition of Canaanite kings. This passage clearly situates it in the north, around Mount Hermon, as a natural landmark marking the extent of the Israelite victory to the northeast. The valley served as a boundary or military and geographical landmark.
H4708J.portee: This place reminds us that God gave Israel specific territories and determined victories. The mention of Mitspa situates God's work within a real and observable geographical framework, showing that His promise of conquest was being fulfilled in the concrete history of the people.

sens: Fortified place in Gilead serving as a lookout point
Region or city in the territory of the tribe of Manasseh
H4708K.detail:
1. Mitspé designates a place located in Gilead, east of the Jordan, which served as a watchtower or observation post. The name itself means "place of surveillance" or "lookout post." It is from there that Jephthah, filled with the Spirit of the Lord, set out to fight the Ammonites (Judges 11:29).
2. This place is associated with the region of Gilead and the territory of Manasseh, forming a strategic geographical ensemble in the lands located beyond the Jordan.
H4708K.origine: The name Mitspé comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to look" or "to observe" — hence the idea of an observation post or watchtower. It is a descriptive place name, given to this location because of its defensive and surveillance function. Several places in Israel bore this name, as it was natural to fortify heights to watch over the surroundings.
H4708K.emploi: Mitspé is mentioned only once in the Bible at this specific location: in Judges 11:29, where it appears as a gathering or rallying point for Jephthah during his campaign against the Ammonites. The text explicitly identifies it as being in Gilead, a key region of the trans-Jordanian lands, and it marks a stage in the military deployment of the judge of Israel.

sens: Fortified city of Gilead, in Transjordan, south of the Jabbok
H4709G.detail: 1. Mitspa is a city built in a high place, on an elevation, which explains its name: the Hebrew word literally means "lookout point" or "place of surveillance." It was a strategic site in Gilead, a mountainous region east of the Jordan, where one could watch the movements of enemies (1 Samuel 7:5-7).
H4709G.origine: The name comes from the Hebrew צפה (tsafah), which means "to look," "to observe from above," hence "to watch." Mitspa designates the place where one watches, an observatory or guard post. This root evokes the image of a sentinel watching over the territory from a high position.
H4709G.emploi: Mitspa appears 31 times in the Bible, mainly in the historical books (Judges, Samuel, Chronicles) and in Jeremiah. It is a place of national assembly: the Israelites gather there before a battle against the Benjaminites (Judges 20:1), Samuel calls Israel there for a religious and military renewal (1 Samuel 7:5-12), Asa fortifies it (2 Chronicles 16:6). Later, it becomes the seat of government after the exile: Gedaliah establishes his administration there and is assassinated there (Jeremiah 40-41). Mitspa symbolizes the civil and religious power of Israel.
H4709G.portee: Mitspa reminds us that God has places where His people gather to be judged, taught, and renewed. It is a landmark in the history of the covenant: a place of prayer, judgment, and obedience, but also of betrayal and ruin when the people stray from it.

sens: Watchtower or observation place in Gilead
Stone cairn erected between Laban and Jacob as a witness of covenant
Camp and seat of power of the Gileadites
Image of the trap or net set against Israel
H4709H.detail:
1. Mitspa literally means "watchtower" or "place of observation": it is a location in Gilead, north of the Jabbok, where one could watch the surroundings. Its name reflects its strategic position.

2. The cairn of Mitspa Laban, built in Genesis 31:49, is a pile of stones that Jacob and Laban erected as witnesses of their covenant and separation: "May the Lord watch over you and me when we are no longer in sight of each other," says Laban. This cairn marks the place where two men mutually entrust themselves to God.

3. Mitspa becomes an important political center during the time of the Judges: it is where the Gileadites gather against the Ammonites (Judges 10:17), and it is at Mitspa that Jephthah is established as leader by the people and the elders (Judges 11:11). Likewise, Jephthah resides there (Judges 11:34).

4. The prophet Hosea uses Mitspa as an image of the trap: "you have been a trap at Mitspa, and a net spread on Tabor" (Hosea 5:1), likely evoking religious or political practices that led Israel away from faithfulness to God.
H4709H.origine: The Hebrew name מִצְפָּה comes from the root צפה (tsapah), which means "to look," "to observe," "to spy"; hence the image of the "place from which one looks" or "watchtower." The same root is found in other Hebrew words related to surveillance. The proper name Mitspa is borne by several places in Israel, but this one in Gilead is the most notable in the accounts of the Judges and the relationships between Jacob and Laban.
H4709H.emploi: Mitspa is a geographical and political place in Gilead, mentioned five times in the Hebrew Bible. It first appears in Genesis 31:49, where Jacob and Laban erect a cairn as a testimony of their covenant and definitive separation. Later, during the time of the Judges, Mitspa becomes a rallying center for military and political purposes: the Gileadites gather there against the Ammonite invasion (Judges 10:17), and it is at Mitspa that Jephthah is appointed leader and where the whole affair of his daughter unfolds (Judges 11:11, 11:34). The prophet Hosea finally uses Mitspa as a symbol of the trap that ensnared Israel, suggesting that this place, once a point of covenant, has become a site of religious compromise (Hosea 5:1).
H4709H.portee: For the Christian reader, Mitspa reminds us that covenants between men, even engraved in stone, remain under the watch of God alone: "May the Lord watch... when we are no longer in sight of each other" (Genesis 31:49). It also shows how a place can transition from faithful covenant to trap: Hosea warns that religion itself can become a net that distances one from the true God. Finally, Mitspa is the stage for the drama of Jephthah, a poignant illustration of how promises made lightly before God lead to irreversible consequences.

sens: Place located at the foot of Mount Hermon
Region inhabited by the Hivites at the time of the conquest of Canaan
H4709I.detail:
1. Mitspa is a geographical location situated at the foot of Mount Hermon, the great mountain in northern Canaan. Its name literally means "watchtower" or "observation post," as it was a high strategic point from which one could survey the area. In Joshua 11:3, this place is mentioned as a region where the Hivites lived at the time of Joshua's conquest of Canaan.
2. Mitspa represents one of the Canaanite territories that Joshua conquered. It is listed alongside other peoples and regions—Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites—to show the extent of Joshua's military campaign in the northern part of the country. It is an important geographical point that marks the boundaries of the territory conquered under God's direction.
H4709I.origine: The Hebrew name מִצְפָּה (Mitspa) comes from the root צפה (tsafah), which means "to observe" or "to spy." This word evokes the idea of a high point from which one watches the horizon—a watchtower. This location was strategically situated at the foot of Mount Hermon, the highest peak in the region, making it an excellent observation post. The name thus reflects its defensive and strategic function in ancient Canaan.
H4709I.emploi: Mitspa is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Joshua 11:3, in the context of Joshua's conquest of Canaan. The passage enumerates the various Canaanite peoples—Canaanites, Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites, Hivites—and their respective regions that were subdued during this campaign. Mitspa is presented as the territory of the Hivites, located "at the foot of Hermon," making it a crucial geographical marker for understanding the extent of the conquest in northern Canaan.

sens: hidden wealth or precious objects
that which is buried and sought to be discovered
that which has value and is kept secret
H4710.detail:
1. The word refers to hidden wealth, precious objects that are kept safe—in the case of Edom, the treasures of wealth that Esau had amassed (Obadiah 1:6: "How are his treasures searched out!"). It is the image of the loot or goods that one conceals.
2. More broadly, it evokes that which is buried or concealed and that one digs to find—something that is not accessible at first glance, which must be sought or unearthed forcefully.
H4710.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "hidden, buried." It is related to other Hebrew words expressing the idea of what is concealed or covered. The initial image is that of something that is buried or covered to protect it.
H4710.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Obadiah 1:6, where it describes the treasures of the Edomites. The prophet Obadiah speaks of the judgment of Edom, asserting that its hidden riches will be discovered and taken away. In this context, "treasure" refers to the goods and resources that a nation accumulates and attempts to protect, but which will be brought to light during divine judgment.
H4710.portee: This word reminds us that no hidden wealth escapes the gaze of God. Even what is buried or thought to be well concealed is visible to the Lord, who can expose it according to His justice.

sens: Extract the juice or liquid from something by pressing or sucking
Taste with delight and pleasure
Fully enjoy a good, a blessing
H4711.detail: 1. The primary meaning of the word is physical: to extract milk or a liquid by sucking or pressing, like a child drinking milk from its mother. It conveys the idea of draining, of drawing all the benefit from a source. 2. However, the Bible uses it figuratively to express the deep and conscious pleasure one derives from something: not merely receiving, but taking the time to taste, to savor (Isaiah 66:11). 3. It is to fully enjoy, with gratitude and attention, the comforts and glory that God offers. The word evokes a joy that is savored slowly, which permeates the one who receives it.
H4711.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that depicts the action of sucking or drawing a liquid: the image is that of an infant nursing from its mother. This root has given rise in Hebrew to words related to nourishment and satisfaction. The term has retained this nuance of pleasure derived from consumption, from complete absorption.
H4711.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 66:11. The prophet describes future salvation using the image of a mother nourishing her children: restored Jerusalem will be like a generous woman whose sons will drink milk with joy. To savor here denotes the attitude of one who receives the comforts and glory of God, not passively, but with conscious pleasure and active gratitude.
H4711.portee: This word teaches us not merely to receive God's blessings, but to truly savor them, to deeply taste their sweetness and reality. It is a call to take the time to enjoy with gratitude what God offers us, rather than living distractedly. For the Christian, it is an invitation to cultivate a conscious joy in the promises and presence of God.

sens: State of intense physical or moral distress
Feeling of being squeezed, suffocated, without an escape
Oppression caused by misfortune or persecution
Anxious fear in the face of danger
H4712.detail:
1. Anguish is primarily an emotion of deep distress that overwhelms the sufferer: in Psalms 116:3, the psalmist speaks of the "anguishes of the grave" that had seized him, meaning the panic and despair in the face of death that surrounded him.
2. The word also evokes the image of being in a narrow space, with no way out: in Psalm 118:5, the one who cries "from the depths of distress" asks God to set him "at large," meaning to take him out of this suffocating vise.
3. Anguish can arise from external oppression: in Lamentations 1:3, Judah is caught "in anguish" by its persecutors, deprived of rest among the enemy nations — here, anguish is the result of servitude and persecution.
H4712.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be narrow," "to squeeze," "to confine." This is why it designates both physical confinement and the moral sensation of being crushed, stuck without the possibility of escape. The same root produces other words expressing constraint and limitation of space.
H4712.emploi: This word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always to depict a situation of profound suffering. In the Psalms, anguish is the state of the believer in the face of death or misfortune, from which only God can deliver him by setting him "at large." In Lamentations, it characterizes the condition of Judah in exile, oppressed and without rest among the nations — here, anguish is the effect of persecution. In all cases, the word expresses the idea of being confined, suffocated, without natural escape.
H4712.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that anguish is not a spiritual weakness but a reality that even the psalmists experienced. It drives one to cry out to God, the only one capable of setting us at large and saving us from the vise that grips us. That is why the Psalms teach not to flee from anguish, but to transform it into prayer.

sens: Inhabitant or citizen of ancient Egypt
Slave or servant of Egyptian origin
Foreigner or person from another culture
H4713.detail:
1. The word simply designates an inhabitant or citizen of Egypt, one of the great peoples of antiquity. It is a name of belonging to a country and a nation. In Genesis 41:55, Pharaoh tells the Egyptians to go to Joseph, meaning all the people of Egypt.
2. The word often applies to servants or slaves from Egypt. In Genesis 39:1-2, Joseph is sold to Potiphar, an Egyptian, which shows a link between Egypt and the world of servitude. In Exodus 2:11, Moses sees an Egyptian striking a Hebrew: this is an ordinary man of the Egyptian people, but in a position of power or authority.
3. The word can also evoke the foreigner, one who does not belong to the people of God. The Egyptians are often distinguished from the Hebrews and Israelites in the Bible, marking a separation of peoples and faith.
H4713.origine: The word comes from the root "Mitsrayim," which means Egypt in Hebrew. The name "Egypt" itself comes from the ancient Qemet, which means "the black one," referring to the fertile land of the Nile, or from two regions: Upper Egypt and Lower Egypt ("double straits"). The adjective "Egyptian" is formed from this same root to designate everything that belongs to this people and this country.
H4713.emploi: The word appears 62 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Genesis and Exodus. In Genesis, it designates the inhabitants of the land where Abraham, Joseph, and his family came or lived (Genesis 12:12, 41:55, 39:1). In Exodus, it describes the Egyptians during the plagues and the exodus: they are threatened by the plagues (Exodus 7:18, 14:9), pursue Israel at the Red Sea (Exodus 14:9), and end up humiliated by God (Exodus 14:17-18). The word does not change meaning, but the context shifts from civil and commercial life (with Joseph) to situations of confrontation and judgment (plagues, exodus).
H4713.portee: For the reader, the word Egyptian reminds us that God acts upon nations and peoples. In the story of Joseph, it shows that a child of God can live among foreigners and maintain his faith. In Exodus, it reveals the power of God who delivers His people from the hand of a foreign power. It is a call to remember that God guides history and protects His own.

sens: Country in northeast Africa bordered by the Nile
Territory of famine and refuge for the patriarchs
Place of Israel's slavery
Power that oppresses the people of God
Contrast between servitude and divine deliverance
H4714G.detail:
1. Egypt is a country in northeast Africa, watered by the Nile, located near the Promised Land (Genesis 12:10 — Abram "went down to Egypt" during a famine). It is a real geographical place where the people can find resources when Canaan lacks food.
2. In the history of the patriarchs, Egypt is often a temporary refuge. Abraham goes there to escape famine (Genesis 12:10), Joseph is sold as a slave there (Genesis 37:36 — "Joseph was brought down to Egypt"), and then Jacob's family settles there to survive (Genesis 46:6).
3. Egypt becomes the place of terrible servitude: Israel experiences slavery under Pharaoh, and the people must be delivered "with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm" (Deuteronomy 26:8). It is there that God's power is manifested against oppression.
4. The Egyptians are presented as a rival political and religious power, governed by Pharaoh who opposes God and His people (Exodus 4:21 — the Lord "would harden Pharaoh's heart").
H4714G.origine: The Hebrew name מִצְרַיִם (Mitsrayim) literally means "the double land" or "the land of the Copts," recalling the historical division of Egypt into Upper and Lower Egypt. The name emphasizes the political unity of a great power.
H4714G.emploi: Egypt appears more than 560 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Genesis and Exodus. It is first a country of refuge for Abraham (Genesis 12:10), then the setting for Joseph's life as a slave and minister of Pharaoh (Genesis 37:36 to 41:57). It then becomes the place of Israel's servitude, which God liberates with wonders (Exodus 1:1 to 18:11). Egypt embodies both oppression and the place where God manifests His saving power. After the exodus, it remains a constant presence in Israel's memory as the symbol of what God has delivered them from.
H4714G.portee: Egypt reminds every believer that God never abandons His people in the face of oppression: the deliverance from Egypt becomes the sign of divine faithfulness and the model for all spiritual liberation. For readers of the Gospels, the journey to Egypt of Jesus' family (Matthew 2) evokes this same divine protection. Egypt teaches that God uses trials and the hands of Pharaoh to shape and prepare His people for freedom.

sens: Son of Ham, ancestor of the peoples of northeast Africa
H4714H.detail: 1. In the biblical genealogy of peoples (Genesis 10), Mitsrayim is one of the sons of Ham, himself a son of Noah. He is presented alongside his brothers Cush, Put, and Canaan. Mitsrayim becomes the ancestral name of the populations that inhabit ancient Egypt and the regions of the Nile.
H4714H.origine: The name Mitsrayim literally means "double land" or "land of the Copts" in Hebrew. This ancestral name also becomes the name of the country of Egypt itself. The same Hebrew word designates both the mythical person and the nation that descends from him, according to the common mode of the Bible: an eponymous ancestor gives his name to his people and territory.
H4714H.emploi: Mitsrayim appears four times in the Bible, only in the genealogies of chapter 10 of Genesis and 1 Chronicles 1. These passages enumerate his descendants: he fathered the Ludim, the Anamim, the Lehabim, the Naphtuhim, and other peoples of the Mediterranean region. It serves a purely genealogical and memorial role: establishing the filiation of the nations known in the ancient world according to biblical tradition.

sens: country in North Africa, northeast of Palestine, traversed by the Nile
H4714I.detail: 1. Egypt is the great country in North Africa located near Palestine. Its inhabitants, the Egyptians, played a central role in biblical history: it is where Joseph was sold into slavery, where the people of Israel experienced slavery, and from where Moses led the Hebrews to deliverance (the Exodus). The name "Egypt" comes from Greek and means "land of the Copts"; the Egyptians themselves called it Kemet, "the black land," referring to the richness of its alluvial soil. The Segond mentions "the sea of Egypt" in Isaiah 11:15, a poetic image of judgment where the Lord dries up the waters as He did in the crossing of the Red Sea.
H4714I.origine: The Hebrew word מִצְרַיִם (Mitsrayim) literally means "double straits" or "two lands," perhaps referring to the two ancient regions of Egypt: Upper Egypt (the Nile valley) and Lower Egypt (the delta). This dual character is embedded in the very name of the country in Semitic tradition.
H4714I.emploi: The word Egypt appears constantly in the Bible, especially in Exodus and the historical books that recount Israel's relations with this great neighbor. The Segond cites Isaiah 11:15, where the prophet announces that the Lord will dry up "the tongue of the sea of Egypt": this passage evokes divine control over the waters, recalling the wonders of the Exodus but projected toward Israel's eschatological future.
H4714I.portee: Egypt in the Bible is primarily the place of slavery, but also of miraculous liberation. It symbolizes both human power and impotence in the face of God's will. For the Christian, remembering Egypt is to remember God's redemptive love for His people and His ability to transform oppression into freedom.

sens: Great country in North Africa, traversed by the Nile, neighbor to Palestine
Southern border of the territory of Israel, marked by a river or a stream
The inhabitants of this country
H4714J.detail:
1. Egypt is the great kingdom of North Africa through which the Nile flows. It is a neighbor and ally of Palestine and plays a major role in biblical history. Its name literally means "land of the Copts."
2. In the texts delimiting the territory, the torrent of Egypt (probably the Wadi Garah or a similar watercourse from Sinai) marks the southern border of Israel. Thus in Joshua 15:4, the southern boundary of Judah runs "to the torrent of Egypt"; this same boundary line appears in Numbers 34:5 and 1 Kings 8:65, where it delineates the territory that God has given to His people.
3. The Egyptians, inhabitants of this land, bear the name of "inhabitants of the double gates" or "two lands" (Upper and Lower Egypt), reflecting the geography of this great country.
H4714J.origine: The Hebrew word mitsrayim literally means "land of the Copts" or "of the fronts" (from the ancient Egyptian word for "double"). It designates the country that the Egyptians called Kemet ("black land") due to the fertile silt of the Nile. The Copts are the descendants of the ancient Egyptians. The plural "Egypt" in French is a translation choice that reflects the importance and extent of this great state.
H4714J.emploi: The word "Egypt" appears six times in the provided usages, always in a specific context: the geographical delimitation of the territory of Israel. Four occurrences (Numbers 34:5, Joshua 15:4 and 15:47, 1 Kings 8:65, 2 Chronicles 7:8) mention the "torrent of Egypt" as the southern limit of the land given to Israel. Isaiah 27:12 uses the expression more poetically to denote the limits of future salvation. Egypt functions here less as the land of Pharaoh's stories and the Exodus than as a geographical reference, a stable and recognized boundary of the ancient world.
H4714J.portee: For the biblical reader, Egypt reminds us that God has established defined limits to the territory of Israel. These boundary references emphasize that salvation does not extend indefinitely, but that God delineates His action in history. They also invite the Christian to recognize that God reigns over the nations and sets their boundaries according to His purpose.

sens: Vessel or hearth in which precious metals are melted for purification
Trial or circumstance that tests a person's faith and heart
Test that reveals the true nature or value of something
H4715.detail:
1. The furnace is a pottery or metal container used in goldsmithing and metallurgy to melt and refine silver or gold: it withstands very high temperatures and allows pure metal to separate from impurities. In Proverbs 17:3, the image of the furnace and the crucible denotes the ordinary tools of the metallurgist who purifies metals.
2. By extension, the furnace becomes in the Bible an image of the trial that purifies and reveals the true nature of the human heart: just as fire destroys the impurities of metal, adversity, temptation, or suffering tests a person's faith and intentions. This is why the Psalmist or Job uses this image to speak of what God allows to test sincerity.
3. The furnace also represents judgment or the test that shows a person's true value: in Proverbs 27:21, it is reputation that serves as a furnace for a man, meaning that his reputation reveals who he truly is.
H4715.origine: The Hebrew word מַצְרֵף (mitsreph) comes from the root צרף (tsaraph), which means "to refine metals" or "to test." This root evokes the action of passing through fire, of being tested by fire to purify. It is related to the verb "to refine" and is also found in contexts where God "tests" or "tries" the people or hearts. The word thus describes the vessel that accomplishes this trial by fire.
H4715.emploi: The word appears twice in the book of Proverbs, always in parallel with the "furnace" (כּוּר, kour). In Proverbs 17:3, the author establishes a comparison: the furnace purifies silver and the crucible purifies gold, but it is the Lord who "tests the hearts." In Proverbs 27:21, the parallel is repeated with a variation: a man is judged according to his reputation as a metal is purified in the furnace. This repetition underscores the importance of this biblical image: the trial reveals the true nature, whether it be that of a metal or a human heart.
H4715.portee: The furnace teaches the Christian that trial is not primarily punishment, but a means of purification and revelation: God allows difficulties so that our faith may be tested and strengthened, and so that our true character may be brought to light. This image comforts us by reminding us that trials have a good intention and an end, like the fire of the furnace that purifies gold without destroying it.

sens: State of decomposition of organic matter
Putrefaction of a plant or harvest
Figuratively: moral degradation or spiritual ruin
H4716.detail:
1. The word denotes the state of decomposition of a matter that rots and disintegrates. It is the concrete image of decay. In Isaiah 5:24, "decay" describes how the root of a plant decomposes and rots, an image of punishment that destroys the foundations.
2. By extension, it applies to the degradation of a harvest, substance, or beauty that deteriorates and becomes foul. In Isaiah 3:24, where the word is translated as "infection," it refers to what was beautiful and fragrant (the perfume, hair, clothing) that will be replaced by marks of shame and decay.
3. In a figurative and spiritual sense, the word paints the inner ruin, moral degradation, and destruction of the people who reject God. Decay becomes the symbol of divine judgment: what seemed solid and beautiful collapses and becomes repugnant.
H4716.origine: The Hebrew word מַק (maq) expresses the idea of something that deteriorates, rots, or falls into disintegration. It comes from a root evoking collapse and dissolution. The term is rare in the Old Testament, which underscores the intensity of the image when it appears: it is used only for the darkest and most destructive situations.
H4716.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the book of Isaiah, a prophet who announces divine judgment. In Isaiah 3:24, it describes the transformation of the people of Judah: what was a source of pride and beauty (perfume, hair, fine clothing) will be replaced by infection and shame. In Isaiah 5:24, it depicts the destruction of the Lord's vines, whose root will be struck by decay. Both usages reinforce the prophetic message: judgment is not merely an external punishment, but an internal destruction, a degradation that corrupts the very foundations.
H4716.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that sin is not an adornment or ornament: it is an inner decay that destroys what is deepest within us. Isaiah's prophecy invites us to take seriously the rupture with God, not as a fleeting lightness, but as a degradation that reaches the roots of our existence. It is a call to return to the word of God before this destruction sets in.

sens: Tool used for striking, especially to drive nails or shape metal
Instrument used to strike, deliver a blow
H4717.detail:
1. The hammer is primarily a practical tool: that of the blacksmith who strikes metal to shape it with repeated blows (Isaiah 44:12), or that of the carpenter who drives nails to securely hold pieces of wood together (Jeremiah 10:4). It is a working instrument, an extension of the arm's strength that transforms matter.
2. By extension, the hammer designates the action of striking itself, the percussion tool that delivers blows. In the account of the construction of the Temple (1 Kings 6:7), the absence of a hammer — and thus the absence of striking noise — creates an atmosphere of silence and respect: the stones were prepared elsewhere, and the edifice rises in peace, without the commotion of a noisy construction site.
H4717.origine: The Hebrew word מַקָּבָה (maq.qa.vah) comes from the root קבה which evokes the action of striking or pounding. It is an instrument defined by its function: that which strikes. The word belongs to a family of tools and weapons whose common characteristic is to deliver a violent and precise blow. In biblical Hebrew, this term primarily designates the tool of the worker.
H4717.emploi: The word hammer appears three times in the Old Testament, always to designate a concrete and functional object. In 1 Kings 6:7, during the construction of the Temple, the absence of a hammer symbolizes the extraordinary and sacred nature of the project, where peace must reign. In Isaiah 44:12, the blacksmith uses the hammer to shape the idol in metal: the text emphasizes the effort and sweat of human labor that produces what should remain reserved for God. In Jeremiah 10:4, it is again a practical object, used with nails to stabilize a wooden idol. The context is always that of manual labor or the making of material objects.
H4717.portee: The hammer in these three passages invites the reader to contemplate human work: the silence of the hammer at the Temple speaks of the harmony that God establishes; the hammer of the blacksmith reminds us that all work requires effort and self-denial; finally, the hammers and nails that secure the idol invite reflection on the vanity of what human hands attempt to solidify in the face of God's eternity. The hammer becomes an image of what shapes the material world, distinct from what comes from God.

sens: Tool used for driving or striking
Instrument of death or execution
H4718A.detail:
1. The hammer is a tool consisting of a head made of wood or metal fixed to a handle, used to drive (nails, stakes) by striking. In the account of Judges 4:21, Jael takes a hammer to drive a stake into the temple of the enemy general Sisera while he sleeps: this is the technical and raw use of the word.
2. By extension, the hammer becomes a weapon of death: Jael uses this domestic tool as a murderous instrument. The word then takes on a darker dimension, that of an object capable of taking life.
H4718A.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to strike" or "to crush." The hammer embodies the idea of a violent, repeated, or powerful blow. A variant, maqava (מַקָּבָה), also exists in the Bible with the same meaning. It is a simple and concrete word that designates the tool as artisans and carpenters knew it in ancient Israel.
H4718A.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 4:21. It is a dramatic moment: Jael, wife of Heber, uses a tent hammer to kill Sisera, the commander of the enemy army of Canaanite Jabin. This event is a turning point in Israel's battle against the Canaanites. The hammer is an ordinary tool, diverted from its daily use to become an instrument of deliverance. This account shows how a simple object can accomplish God's work.
H4718A.portee: This passage invites us to meditate on how God uses humble and ordinary means to accomplish His will. Jael's hammer reminds us that victory does not come from conventional military strength, but from the faithfulness and courage of those who trust in God. For the Christian, it is an invitation not to underestimate what God can do with the simple resources He gives us.

sens: Cavity hollowed out in stone or earth
Excavation or mine hole
Pit or well
Figuratively, origin or source (that from which one comes)
H4718B.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a cavity or hole dug into rock or soil — an excavation that goes downwards. This is the primary and concrete meaning of the word.
2. In a work context, it can also evoke a mine or quarry: a place where one digs to extract stone or minerals.
3. It also applies to a pit, a well: any natural or artificial hollow that is embedded in the earth.
4. Figuratively, the hollow becomes an image of origin, the source from which one comes — that which has shaped us. This is in the sense that Isaiah 51:1 asks the people: "Look to the rock from which you were hewn, and to the hole of the pit from which you were dug." The prophet reminds that God drew Israel from the rough stone, like a block extracted from a quarry; the "hollow" is the pit from which this block comes, the modest place and condition of the origin of the chosen people.
H4718B.origine: The Hebrew word maqqqevet derives from a root meaning to dig or to hollow out a hole. It is related to other words that denote the action of piercing, of making a hollow. The image is very physical: that of the tool sinking into the material and leaving an empty space, a cavity.
H4718B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 51:1. It is used there to evoke the original poverty of the people of Israel — not a moral poverty, but a lowly, humble condition from which God drew them. The prophet contrasts the darkness of this pit with the current greatness of Israel and with the call to justice and to seek the Lord: you come from a hollow, from a pit, yet you are called to pursue justice. It is a pedagogical nudge: do not forget your modest origins and what God has done for you.
H4718B.portee: This word invites the believer to remember their spiritual starting point — often marked by unworthiness, sin, or simply profound weakness. It reminds us that God draws us from this "hollow," from this void or moral pit, to elevate us and call us to a righteous life. It is a surge of gratitude and humility in the face of divine grace.

sens: city of Judah in southern Canaan
cave where the defeated kings hid
H4719.detail:
1. Makkéda is a fortified city in southern Canaan, conquered by Joshua during the military campaign against the Canaanite kings (Joshua 10:28). It was located near Beth-Horon and Libna, along the routes that the Israelite armies traveled while pursuing their enemies (Joshua 10:10, 10:29).
2. The city is particularly famous for a cave where five Canaanite kings had taken refuge after their defeat by the Israelites. Joshua discovered them there, brought them out, and executed them (Joshua 10:16-17, 10:21). This place became a symbol of Israel's victory and the fulfillment of God's will in the conquest.
H4719.origine: The name means "place of shepherds" or "shepherds' enclosure" in Hebrew, evoking a protected space intended to shelter livestock. The suffix and form indicate a defined place or space. Makkéda carries the image of a remote, mountainous, and fortified area, suitable for both grazing and defensive retreat.
H4719.emploi: Makkéda appears about nine times in the book of Joshua, primarily in chapter 10, which details the capture and execution of the five kings. It also appears in lists of conquered cities (Joshua 12:16 and 15:41). All uses focus on the narrative of the conquest of Canaan, giving Makkéda a strategic role: it is where the pursuit of the enemies stopped, where the fate of the defeated kings was sealed, and where Joshua regrouped his troops before continuing to other cities.
H4719.portee: Makkéda reminds the reader that Israel's victory is not only military but divine: it is the Lord Himself who "threw them into confusion" (Joshua 10:10). The narrative also shows the importance of total obedience to God and the execution of the judgment promised on the nations that oppose His plan. For the believer, Makkéda illustrates how God fulfills His promises in a precise and unstoppable manner.

sens: Place consecrated to God, where worship is rendered
Building or sacred place of the tabernacle or temple
Most holy inner space, inaccessible to the people
Figure of God's presence among His people
H4720.detail:
1. The sanctuary is primarily a space that God sets apart, which is consecrated for His service and worship. It is a place separated from the rest, reserved for God alone (Leviticus 19:30). The word evokes the idea of separation, of holiness: one cannot enter there casually, nor do anything there carelessly.
2. In the Hebrew Bible, the sanctuary concretely refers to the tabernacle or the temple — the entire edifice where God symbolically dwells among His people. Exodus 25:8 speaks of the sanctuary that God commands to be built; Psalms 78:69 describes it as the dwelling established by God.
3. In a narrower sense, the sanctuary can be the most holy place, the heart of the temple or tabernacle where no one can enter except the high priest, once a year (Ezekiel 45:3). It is the most sacred, most protected area.
4. Spiritually, the sanctuary symbolizes the living presence of God among His people (Ezekiel 37:26-28); to profane or destroy it is to reject this presence and break the covenant.
H4720.origine: The Hebrew word מִקְדָּשׁ (miqddash) comes from the root קדש (qdsh), which means "to be separated, set apart, sacred." A sanctuary is thus a place "set apart," consecrated to God in contrast to the profane. It is the same theme as "holy" (qadosh) and "holiness" (qodshe): it always involves the idea of sacred separation.
H4720.emploi: The word miqddash appears about 70 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Law (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers), the Psalms, and the prophets (particularly Ezekiel). In the Law, it refers to the tabernacle and the purification rules necessary to access it (Leviticus 12:4, 21:12); the priests are its guardians and responsible for the sins committed within (Numbers 18:1). The Psalms celebrate the sanctuary as the house of God, a source of strength and reverence (Psalms 68:36, 73:17). The prophets, especially Ezekiel, denounce the profanation of the sanctuary by sin and disobedience (Ezekiel 5:11, 28:18) and announce its restoration in future times (Ezekiel 37:26-28, 43:21). The word can also apply to illegitimate sanctuaries or foreign altars (Amos 7:9).
H4720.portee: For the believer, the sanctuary reminds us that God demands holiness — not out of legalism, but out of respect for His presence. It is a place of encounter between God and His people; to enter it is to place oneself under His lordship. For the Christian, the body of believers replaces this physical sanctuary: the people of God themselves become the place where God dwells (see 1 Corinthians 3:16-17). This transformation reminds us that the relationship with God no longer depends on a building, but on the heart.

sens: Group of people gathered together
Gathering of believers assembled for worship
Choir or musical group in the context of the temple
H4721.detail:
1. An assembly is a group of people who come together, usually in the same place and for a specific reason. It is literally a crowd or multitude gathered.
2. In a religious context, it refers to the gathering of believers who come together to worship God and participate in temple worship. David says, "I will bless the Lord in the assemblies" (Psalms 26:12), which shows that these meetings are special moments for publicly praising God.
3. The word can also refer to a group of singers or a musical ensemble, as in the context of the temple, assemblies often included sacred songs and music. Psalms 68:27 invites to "bless God in the assemblies," emphasizing the collective and joyful nature of these moments.
H4721.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to gather" or "to convene." It designates the action of bringing together, and by extension, the group that is gathered. The word belongs to the family of Hebrew words related to convocation and community gathering, which are very important in the religious life of Israel.
H4721.emploi: This word appears twice in the Psalms, always in the plural form ("assemblies"), and only in contexts of praise and worship. In Psalms 26:12, David expresses his joy in being able to bless the Lord among the gathered believers. In Psalms 68:27, the invitation to bless God in the assemblies shows that these gatherings are central occasions in the communal faith life of Israel. The word always emphasizes the collective and public aspect of worship, never solitary devotion.
H4721.portee: This word reminds Christians that praising and worshiping God is not strictly a personal affair: it gains its full strength when experienced together, in an assembly of believers. Whether at church on Sunday or in other Christian gathering contexts, we are invited to bless God "in the assemblies," in communion with our brothers and sisters. It is an invitation to value community life and shared worship.

sens: Station where the Israelites camped during the Exodus
H4722.detail: 1. Makhéloth is a place mentioned in the account of the Israelites' journey in the desert after leaving Egypt. It is a stop in their journey, where they camped before continuing to other destinations (Numbers 33:25-26).
H4722.origine: The name Makhéloth literally means "place of assembly" or "gathering," formed from the Hebrew root that designates an assembly or a multitude gathered. It evokes the idea of a place where the people could come together — appropriate for a stop in the journey where the entire community camped together.
H4722.emploi: Makhéloth appears only twice in the Bible, both in chapter 33 of Numbers, which lists the forty-two stops of the Israelites' journey in the desert between Egypt and the Promised Land. The station is mentioned between Haradah and Tahath in this itinerary list. No particular event is recorded there; it is simply a waypoint in the people's march toward Canaan.
H4722.portee: This place reminds us that God's people, in their exodus, needed regular stops to rest and gather. Each stop in the desert is accounted for by God, who guides His people step by step toward the promise. It is an encouragement to recognize divine direction in the daily life, even during passages we do not understand.

sens: Region of Cilicia from which the horses imported by Solomon came
H4723A.detail: Koué is a region of ancient Asia Minor (modern Cilicia, in Turkey) that was famous for breeding high-quality horses. King Solomon imported horses from there for his royal cavalry, which reflects his distant trade relations and wealth (1 Kings 10:28 and 2 Chronicles 1:16 both mention these "horses from Koué").
H4723A.origine: The name Koué designates a well-attested historical region in Egyptian and Hittite sources under variations of the same name. The region was renowned in antiquity for its excellent horses, which explains why Solomon made his purchases there.
H4723A.emploi: Koué appears twice in the Bible, always in relation to the horse trade during Solomon's reign. The two occurrences (1 Kings 10:28 and its parallel 2 Chronicles 1:16) describe exactly the same reality: Solomon bought his horses from merchants who brought them from Koué. These horses were part of his great prosperity and political influence.

sens: Confident expectation for the future, assurance that a happy thing will happen
That in which one places their trust, object or person that inspires confidence
Source of trust and comfort in difficult times
Situation or condition of one who keeps hope alive
H4723B.detail:
1. Hope is primarily the expectation that something good will happen. It is a forward-looking confidence, the inner assurance that one is not abandoned. In 1 Chronicles 29:15, David says that our days on earth are like a shadow and that there is no hope — he expresses the total absence of happy certainty in light of the brevity of life.
2. The word also designates the person or thing in which one places their hope, that which becomes our refuge. In Jeremiah 14:8 and 17:13, God Himself is called the hope of Israel: He is the solid foundation on which the people can rely, especially when everything seems lost.
3. In times of crisis or distress, hope becomes that strength which prevents despair. Ezra 10:2 states that after sin, "Israel is not left without hope" — there is always a possible way out, a path to restoration.
4. Hope characterizes the condition of one who has not given up, who keeps an open way ahead. It stands in opposition to despair, to abandonment without recourse.
H4723B.origine: The Hebrew word miqveh comes from a root that means to wait, to hope. The same word also designates a cistern, a reservoir of water — an image that sheds light on the meaning: just as a cistern holds the water essential for life, hope is what holds, that in which we gather and that we keep jealously. This is why Jeremiah 17:13 compares God to a fountain of living water: He is the inexhaustible source of hope, while abandoning Him would be like renouncing one's well of life.
H4723B.emploi: The word appears five times in the Old Testament, mainly in the prophecies of Jeremiah and in the accounts of Ezra and Chronicles. It is used in three ways: as absence of hope in the face of human fragility (1 Chronicles 29:15), as persistence of hope despite sin (Ezra 10:2), and especially as identification of God Himself as the source and foundation of hope (Jeremiah 14:8; 17:13; 50:7). In the three passages from Jeremiah, the context is one of distress — exile, judgment, loss — and it is precisely there that God is recognized as hope: the source that never runs dry, even in the heart of disaster.
H4723B.portee: For the believer, understanding that God is our hope changes everything. It is not a mere human confidence, uncertain and fragile, but an anchoring in the unshakeable character of God. Even when everything collapses, when one feels foreign and fragile on this earth as David expresses, God remains hope — the one who saves us in times of distress. This is why biblical hope is firm: it does not depend on our circumstances, but on the faithfulness of the one who promises us a future.

sens: Collection, natural or artificial accumulation of water
Reservoir or basin containing water
Water gathered in one place, forming a mass
Set or totality of concentrated water
H4723C.detail:
1. The word designates any collection of water gathered in one place: seas, lakes, reservoirs, or cisterns. It is water that accumulates naturally or is intentionally collected. In Genesis 1:10, God calls the seas "masses"—that is, all the salty waters gathered on earth after creation.
2. By extension, it designates a reservoir or a basin designed to collect and store water. In Leviticus 11:36, cisterns (dug reservoirs) and springs (natural masses of water) are distinguished from vessels, which shows that a mass is a significant accumulation of water in a fixed location.
3. The word emphasizes the idea of mass or totality: it is the entirety of unified waters, not dispersed. In Exodus 7:19, all the "masses of waters" of Egypt (rivers, streams, ponds) must be struck as a single entity, demonstrating the unity of the concept.
H4723C.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to hope" or "to wait," but in this context, it evokes the idea of gathering or concentration. It is related to the notion of collection or accumulation. The word reflects the concrete image of water accumulating and standing still in one place, as opposed to flowing or dispersing water.
H4723C.emploi: The word appears three times in the Old Testament, always to designate collections of water. In Genesis 1:10, it is the first act of creation: God gathers the waters under the sky and calls them "seas." In Exodus 7:19, during the plagues of Egypt, all the masses of waters (rivers, streams, ponds) turn to blood. In Leviticus 11:36, springs and cisterns (pure masses of water) are contrasted with vessels (which can be contaminated). The word thus designates both natural waters and constructed reservoirs, but always a stable and defined accumulation.
H4723C.portee: This word reminds us that water, a vital resource and symbol of life in the Bible, is the work of God. It does not flow randomly: it is gathered, ordered, and entrusted to humanity. Particularly in the purity laws of Leviticus, this mass of water marks the boundary between what can be purified and what remains defiled, inviting the believer to see God's created order as a framework of holiness.

sens: basin or cistern intended to collect and store water
accumulation of water retained and stored
vital resource depending on divine providence
H4724.detail:
1. The reservoir is a dug or constructed basin for collecting and keeping water, especially in areas where it is scarce. In Isaiah 22:11, the inhabitants of Jerusalem under threat dig reservoirs between the city walls to ensure their survival in case of siege.
2. The word also designates the mass of water itself, the collected accumulation: it is the water retained in the basin, ready to be used. This amassed water represents a provision, a reserve.
3. The prophetic text gives this reservoir a spiritual dimension: people are concerned about their material reserves but forget the One who disposes of all things. The reservoir becomes an image of our human efforts and our forgetfulness of God.
H4724.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to gather, collect." It is close to words expressing the idea of collection or accumulation. The concept of a water reservoir was common in Israel and the ancient Near East, where water was precious and required facilities to be preserved. This word appears rarely in the Bible, reflecting its technical and specialized use.
H4724.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 22:11. Isaiah uses this term in a vision of the last days of Jerusalem before captivity. The inhabitants make material reserves by digging reservoirs, an action that is wise and prudent in itself. But the prophet sees a spiritual tragedy in this: these material preparations are accompanied by total blindness to God's will. It is an ordinary water reservoir that becomes a symbol of the absurdity of human plans that ignore the Lord.
H4724.portee: This word confronts us with a permanent question: on what do we base our security? Material reserves are not bad in themselves, but they become dangerous when they blind us to divine providence. Isaiah invites us to seek the Lord first, not to secure ourselves by our own strength. The reservoir reminds us that all provision comes from God and that true wisdom consists in recognizing and fearing Him.

sens: Physical location, defined space where something is found or occurs
Station, post, function assigned to someone
Dwelling, residence of a person
Region, country, land
Empty space, capacity to contain something
H4725.detail:
1. A place is primarily a concrete physical location, an identifiable portion of space. Genesis 1:9 illustrates this when God says, "Let the waters gather in one place": He designates the space where the waters will concentrate, thus creating dry land. This is the most basic and frequent meaning in the Bible.
2. The place can also be a post or station assigned to someone—a function or role in an established order. Genesis 40:3 speaks of the "place where the prisoners were kept": it is both the location and the specific role of the guards and prisoners in this context.
3. The place is also the dwelling, the home where one lives. Job 7:10 says, "the place he inhabited will know him no more": it is the house, the domestic space that becomes a symbol of a person's continuity. Leviticus 6:18 mentions the "place where the burnt offering is slaughtered," the designated area for worship.
4. The word expands to designate an entire region, a territory, a country. Deuteronomy 26:2 speaks of the "place that the Lord your God will choose": it refers to the sanctuary at the heart of the given territory, but also to the land itself.
5. In a figurative or less common sense, the place can mean empty space, the available spot, or capacity. Jeremiah 7:32 mentions that "they will bury the dead in Topheth because there is no place": here the word designates the physical capacity, the space that is lacking.
H4725.origine: The word מָקוֹם (maqom) derives from a Hebrew root קוּם (qoum) meaning "to rise," "to stand up." The place is thus originally "that on which one stands," the spot where one stands or takes position. This etymology explains why the word can also mean "station" or "post": it is where one "stands." The word shares this root with other Hebrew terms evoking permanence, establishment, and stability.
H4725.emploi: The word maqom appears about 379 times in the Old Testament, making it an extremely common word. It is used in all books and contexts: creation (Genesis 1:9), the movements of Abraham and Jacob (Genesis 12-35), the prescriptions of worship (Leviticus and Numbers), historical accounts, and laments. In the laws, the word designates precisely where a ritual act must take place (slaughtering an animal, presenting an offering). In narratives, it marks the stages of a day or a journey. Over time, "the place" comes to designate the sanctuary itself—the spot that God has chosen for His name (Deuteronomy 26:2)—which enriches the word with a central religious and symbolic significance for the life of Israel.
H4725.portee: Understanding the word "place" helps the reader grasp how the Bible anchors faith in the real and the concrete. God acts in specific places, establishes His worship in a particular location, promises the land as a place of possession and rest. The place is never trivial in the Bible: it is where God reveals Himself (Mount Sinai, the temple) and where man responds (the altar, the home). This attention to the concrete reminds the Christian that faith does not soar into the abstract but is rooted in history, territory, and ordinary life. It is also an invitation to recognize the places where God acts today.

sens: Fountain or natural water point springing from the ground
The origin, the primary cause from which something flows
Life, health, purification (in a figurative sense)
The source of wisdom and teaching
Flow of blood or bodily discharge
H4726.detail: 1. A source is primarily a natural fountain, a water point that springs from the ground — this is the most concrete meaning. 2. Figuratively, the word denotes the origin or primary cause from which something flows: it is that from which a reality comes and flows. 3. In particular, Scripture speaks of the "source of life" (Psalms 36:10) to refer to the Lord Himself, who gives and sustains life, just as a spring provides water. 4. The wisdom and teaching of the wise are also sources of life (Proverbs 13:14; Proverbs 16:22), as they keep one away from deadly traps. 5. The word can also refer to a bodily flow: in Leviticus 12:7, it speaks of the flow of blood after childbirth, which renders the woman ritually impure until purification.
H4726.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that fundamentally means "to dig" or "to excavate." A source is what springs forth when one digs into the earth: it is the point of emergence. The natural image of springing forth gives the word its strength: just as water perpetually flows from a source, life, wisdom, and blessing spring forth from God.
H4726.emploi: The word appears seventeen times in the Old Testament, mainly in the wisdom books (Proverbs, Psalms) and among the prophets (Jeremiah, Hosea, Zechariah). Its usage evolves from the physical to the spiritual. Initially concrete in Leviticus (bodily flow), it quickly becomes figurative: the source becomes an image of the origin of all good. God is the source of life (Psalms 36:10), wisdom is a source of life (Proverbs 13:14; Proverbs 16:22), and the teaching of the wise is also (Proverbs 10:11). Sin dries up the source: Jeremiah compares idolatry to "forsaking the fountain of living water" (Jeremiah 2:13), that is, a rejection of God Himself. The source can also be polluted or troubled, like the righteous who stumbles (Proverbs 25:26), thus losing its effectiveness. Zechariah 13:1 promises an "open fountain" for sin and impurity, an image of eschatological purification.
H4726.portee: This word invites the believer to seek in God, not in their own resources, the source of life, wisdom, and purification. It reminds that no human well can quench the thirst of the soul: only communion with God, the living source, provides lasting life and protection against spiritual death. It is an invitation not to "forsake the fountain of living water" to dig our own broken cisterns.

sens: The act of receiving something as a gift or payment
The act of welcoming a gift or reward
The reception of a present offered to influence a decision
H4727.detail:
1. This word designates the simple act of receiving something that is offered to you — a gift, a present, a payment. It is the action of taking what is given to you.

2. In the biblical context, especially regarding justice, it takes on a more precise nuance: it describes the acceptance of a gift or bribe intended to influence a decision. King Jehoshaphat forbids his judges from accepting gifts, as this can corrupt them and lead them away from justice (2 Chronicles 19:7). This is why the word carries a moral tone: accepting gifts risks losing one's impartiality.
H4727.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root קחח (qachach, "to take," "to seize"). The same root is found in verbs that mean to take, receive, or accept. Here, the word specifically denotes the act of taking or receiving; in the judicial context, it evokes the danger of "taking" what one should not — a gift that could distort judgment.
H4727.emploi: This word appears only once in biblical Hebrew, in the context of King Jehoshaphat's speech to his judges. It carries an ethical charge: it is about prohibiting the acceptance of gifts as a means of corruption. The image is that of a judge who, instead of remaining upright and impartial, "takes" a gift and allows his judgment to be affected. This judicial context gives the word its full significance: receiving is commonplace, but accepting a gift to sway justice is an abomination.
H4727.portee: This word reminds the believer, and particularly those in positions of responsibility (magistrate, pastor, leader), that impartiality is a sacred duty. Accepting a gift that could influence a just decision is to betray the trust placed in oneself and offend God. It is a call to absolute righteousness, without compromise with corruption, no matter how small.

sens: material goods offered for sale or exchange
product or commodity that is sold
H4728.detail:
1. Merchandise is any good that is brought to sell or exchange: it is an object that one possesses and offers to others for profit. In Nehemiah 10:31, the Israelites commit not to buy merchandise on the Sabbath and during festivals, even from foreign merchants who would offer them for sale.
2. More broadly, this term designates any product or commodity — food, fabrics, utensils — that a seller offers to the public. It encompasses everything that is sold on the market, equivalent to our words "items" or "goods" when talking about commerce.
H4728.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of seizing, taking in hand, which fits well with merchandise that one grabs to examine or buy. The form with the doubling of consonants reinforces the idea of something concrete and tangible. It is a noun formed to designate the object of commercial exchange.
H4728.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Nehemiah 10:31. It is found in the solemn commitment that the people of Israel make after returning from exile: to respect the Sabbath by refusing to buy merchandise, even if foreign merchants bring them to sell at the gates of Jerusalem on holy days. The context shows that it refers to any goods or commodities, without specific mention — everything that is sold.
H4728.portee: This verse reminds believers that the Sabbath rest is not a mere pause, but a consecration of time to God, incompatible with the hustle of commerce. Refusing to buy, even desirable or useful things, expresses a priority: God before business. For us, it invites us to examine how our time and resources truly reflect what matters most.

sens: table or altar on which incense is burned
place from which the fragrant smoke of incense rises to God
symbol of prayer ascending to heaven
