H4729.detail: 1. The word concretely designates a table or a small altar intended to receive incense, which burns and produces fragrant smoke. In Exodus 30:1, God commands Moses to make this altar of acacia wood, a piece of furniture in the tabernacle reserved for this specific use. 2. It is the place from which the fragrant curls of smoke rise to heaven, visible and tangible, from the burning perfume. This ascending smoke represents an act of worship, an offering that pleases God. 3. The incense burned on this altar becomes in the Bible the image of prayer that rises from the believer's heart to God: an invisible yet precious offering, pleasing and powerful.
H4729.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes combustion and smoke — literally a place where something burns and smokes. This root is present in several Hebrew words related to fire and incense. The concept dates back to the practices of worship in the tabernacle and temple, where incense held a central and symbolic place in the relationship with God.
H4729.emploi: The word appears only once in the preserved Hebrew Bible, in Exodus 30:1, where God gives precise instructions for making this altar of incense. It is a well-defined liturgical piece of furniture, distinct from the altar of burnt offerings. This altar was placed inside the tabernacle, in the holy place, before the veil that separated the people from the most holy place. Its unique use underscores the ritual and symbolic importance of incense in Israelite worship.
H4729.portee: This altar represents for the believer a powerful symbol: the prayer and intercession that ascend to God in a pleasing and effective manner. Just as the incense burns to spread its fragrance, the believer offers to God their prayer, worship, and heart. It is a reminder that our worship, our prayer must be intentional, regular, and pleasing to God.

sens: Container used to burn incense during worship
Liturgical utensil held by priests during rites
H4730.detail:
1. The censer is a small container, often made of metal, designed to burn incense during religious ceremonies. It is an object of Jewish worship that produces fragrant smoke intended to rise to God. In 2 Chronicles 26:19, King Uzziah, who was not a priest, dares to take the censer to burn incense himself before the altar of incense — which provokes God's anger and he is struck with leprosy on his forehead.
2. The censer is a utensil that each person holds in hand during worship. In Ezekiel 8:11, seventy elders of Israel stand "each with a censer in hand," burning incense before idols in the temple — a vision that denounces Israel's unfaithfulness to God. It is therefore an object directly handled by the officiant.
H4730.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to burn" or "to smoke." The censer is the utensil that produces the smoke of the incense, hence its name. It is a specifically liturgical object, related to temple worship.
H4730.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in a temple worship context: first in the prophet Ezekiel (8:11) who sees elders burning incense before idols, and then in Chronicles (26:19) when King Uzziah commits the sacrilege of wanting to burn incense himself. In both cases, the censer is at the heart of a religious act: legitimate when used by the priest, but a grave transgression when taken by a non-priest.
H4730.portee: The censer reminds us that worship has its rules and designated officiants. No one can approach God in any manner: in Israel, only the priest had the right to burn incense. The case of Uzziah teaches that even royalty cannot ignore the limits that God has set for worship. The censer is therefore a symbol of regulated access to the divine presence.

sens: long and rigid object, generally made of wood, held in hand
stick or branch of a tree
object of power or authority, symbol of power or command
shepherd's instrument to guide or strike the flock
H4731.detail:
1. It is primarily a simple wooden object: a stick that can be held, struck, or carried. Jacob crosses the Jordan with his stick in hand (Genesis 32:10), Balaam strikes his donkey with a stick (Numbers 22:27), David takes simple sticks to confront Goliath (1 Samuel 17:40).
2. The word also refers to the branch or stem of a living tree. Jacob takes green branches of poplar and peels them to obtain white strips (Genesis 30:37).
3. The stick becomes a symbol of authority and power: Jeremiah speaks of a "majestic stick" that is broken, an image of the power of a kingdom or a leader that collapses (Jeremiah 48:17).
4. For the shepherd, it is the specific instrument that guides and corrects the flock. Zechariah refers to it as the emblem of the true shepherd (Zechariah 11:7-14).
H4731.origine: The Hebrew word maqquel comes from a root that means "to strike" or "to be strong." It refers to the idea of an object that serves to strike or impose, hence its connection to power and authority. The same root generates other words associated with power or evil. The word evokes the concrete image of the stick as a tool of control and action.
H4731.emploi: This word appears 16 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the narratives of Genesis and in the prophets. It designates either a practical everyday object (the traveler's stick, the shepherd's tool) or a branch or green stem. As one progresses through the Bible, the meaning deepens: the stick becomes the image of political or religious power, of the command of a king or a prophet. In Zechariah, the double stick of the shepherd symbolizes the two aspects of leading the people. Jeremiah uses it to evoke the fall of a power.
H4731.portee: This word teaches that authority and governance can be represented by a simple material object. It invites the believer to meditate on the stick as a symbol of the divine shepherd who guides his people, as reminded by the image of the shepherd with his staff. It is also a reminder that true power is not in appearance, but in the ability to lead and correct with justice.

sens: Son of Jehiel, prince or chief of Gibeon, of the tribe of Benjamin
H4732G.detail: Mikloth is a character from the Old Testament, son of Jehiel and Maacah, of the tribe of Benjamin. He lived during the time of the united monarchy of Israel. He is mentioned in the genealogies of Chronicles as a Benjamite living in Jerusalem alongside his brothers (1 Chronicles 8:32). Mikloth had a son named Shimeam (or Shimea), whose name also appears in the genealogical records. In 1 Chronicles 9:37, he is cited among the family heads responsible, alongside Gedor, Ahijah, and Zechariah, indicating his role in community responsibility. Some ancient sources also designate him as the chief of the second division of King David's army, a military role attested during the time of the Israelite monarchy.
H4732G.origine: The name Mikloth literally means "sticks" or "stems" in Hebrew (from the root referring to what is straight or pointed). It is a personal name formed from a concrete image, common in Hebrew onomastics. The name may reflect a quality of firmness or uprightness expected of the bearer, important traits for a family head or military officer.
H4732G.emploi: Mikloth appears three times in Chronicles, exclusively in the genealogies of Benjamin. In 1 Chronicles 8:32, he is presented as the son of Jehiel and father of Shimea, and it is noted that he lived in Jerusalem with his family. The same passage is repeated in 1 Chronicles 9:37-38 with a slight spelling variation (his son is called Shimeam there), indicating that these texts preserve the genealogical records of the tribe during the return from exile. His inclusion in these lists suggests that he was an important figure in the administrative and familial history of Benjamin, although the details of his life are not developed beyond these genealogies.

sens: military chief during the divided monarchy of Israel
officer of the second division of David's army
H4732H.detail: Mikloth is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time of the military organization of King David's kingdom. He held a position of responsibility in the royal army: he was one of the chiefs of the second division, commanded by Dodaï the Ahohite, which consisted of twenty-four thousand men (1 Chronicles 27:4). His role was therefore to assist the division chief in the command and administration of this significant contingent.
H4732H.origine: The name Mikloth means "sticks" or "little sticks" in Hebrew, derived from the word "maqèl" which designates a stick, a cane, or a rod. This name, formed from an image of strength and authority (the stick of the chief), was borne by this military dignitary during David's time. There was also another Mikloth from a different family, mentioned as the son of Jehiel and a Benjamite, but this is not the same individual.
H4732H.emploi: Mikloth appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:4. This passage lists the chiefs of the twelve military divisions that David had organized, each consisting of twenty-four thousand warriors. Mikloth is mentioned there as subordinate to Dodaï the Ahohite, chief of the second division. This brief mention shows that he was a reliable officer in the administrative and military system established by David to strengthen and manage his kingdom.

sens: City where an unintentional murderer could take refuge to escape the avenger of blood
Legal and protected asylum for someone who committed a murder without intent
Protection offered by divine law against private vengeance
H4733.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a special city established by the law of Moses, where someone who had killed someone unintentionally could flee and be protected. Israel had six: three in Transjordan and three in Canaan (Numbers 35:6). These cities were given to the Levites and served as legal sanctuaries.
2. The person who took refuge in this city was protected as long as the high priest lived; upon his death, they could return home without risk (Numbers 35:28). It was a protection against the personal vengeance of the victim's relative (Joshua 20:3).
3. The refuge thus represents the grace of God that distinguishes between voluntary murder (a serious crime) and accidental killing (lesser responsibility). The law protects those who did not act with criminal intent.
H4733.origine: The Hebrew word miqlaṭ comes from the root qlaṭ which means "to flee" or "to escape." It literally designates a "place of flight." It is a place of escape, an asylum. The concept appears mainly in the legislative passages of Exodus and Leviticus that organize the life of Israel.
H4733.emploi: The word miqlaṭ appears 20 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in penal law passages: Numbers 35 (which defines these cities), Joshua 20 (which recounts their establishment), and 1 Chronicles 6 (which lists them). These cities of refuge embody a key principle of Israelite justice: the distinction between unintentional homicide and deliberate murder. Only the unintentional murderer could take refuge there; the intentional murderer had to be delivered to the avenger of blood (Numbers 35:12). The refuge ceased upon the death of the high priest, highlighting the link between human justice and the priesthood.
H4733.portee: These cities of refuge reveal God's mercy toward someone who commits an offense without criminal intent. They teach Christians that God does not confuse accident with voluntary moral guilt, and that He offers protection to those fleeing vengeance. They also remind us that justice must be just: protecting the innocent or the unintentional wrongdoer while holding the criminal accountable.

sens: Engraved or chiseled work in wood, stone, or metal
Ornamental motif carved in relief or in hollow on a surface
Interior decoration of a temple or building
H4734.detail:
1. This word designates a work of engraving or chiseling — a technique where the artisan carves or shapes a hard surface (wood, stone, metal) to create a motif. In 1 Kings 6:18, the cedar wood of Solomon's temple is adorned with "sculptures" of gourds and blooming flowers.
2. The visible result is an ornamental motif, a decoration: these sculptures create forms that appear in relief or in hollow. In 1 Kings 6:29, Solomon has cherubim, palms, and blooming flowers sculpted on the walls of the temple, both inside and outside.
3. In the context of the temple, the word also simply designates the interior decor, the ornament that beautifies the sacred walls and furniture. In 1 Kings 7:31, the bases of the bronze sea also bear "sculptures" that embellish them.
H4734.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to dig" or "to excavate." It literally designates the result of this action: what has been carved into a material to bring forth a shape. It is a precise artisanal work, common in the workshops of the ancient Near Eastern kingdoms.
H4734.emploi: The word appears 4 times in 1 Kings, always to describe the ornaments of Solomon's temple and its furniture. In 1 Kings 6:18 and 6:29, it refers to the sculptures that cover the interior of the temple: gourds, flowers, cherubim. In 1 Kings 7:31, it adorns the base of the bronze sea. The word emphasizes the attention to detail and the beauty of artisanal work in the sacred edifice. Sometimes translated as "interior" when referring to the space where the sculptures are located, rather than the engraved object itself.
H4734.portee: These sculptures remind us that true worship of God is also expressed through beauty and care: the temple is not an ordinary building, but a place where artistic excellence reflects the honor due to God. The abundance of ornaments shows Solomon's generous heart in building the house of the Lord. These human works, crafted with art, contribute to the splendor of the worship rendered to God.

sens: Group of domesticated animals raised together: cattle, sheep, goats, camels, donkeys.
Wealth measured in livestock, a form of property and prestige in pastoral culture.
Acquired or possessed property, object of commercial transaction.
H4735.detail:
1. The flock is primarily a group of domesticated animals raised together in pasture. Genesis 4:20 presents Jabal as "the father of those who dwell in tents and have livestock," showing that livestock raising goes hand in hand with nomadic life. In Exodus 9:3, during the plagues of Egypt, God strikes "your livestock that are in the fields," meaning the animals in pasture.
2. The flock represents the main wealth in the ancient biblical world. In Genesis 34:23, the men of Shechem speak of the flocks as coveted wealth: "Their livestock, their goods, and all their cattle, will they not be ours?" In Joshua 22:8, the tribes returning to their lands are told they come back "with great wealth, with very large flocks."
3. The flock can also refer to a purchased or possessed good, an object of exchange. In Exodus 34:19, God tells Israel: "Every firstborn belongs to me, even every male firstborn among your livestock of the herd and the flock," thus establishing His right of ownership over what Israel possesses.
H4735.origine: The Hebrew word miqneh comes from the root qanah, which means "to buy, acquire, possess." The flock is literally what one acquires and possesses — the word emphasizes the relationship of ownership. This root is found in other Hebrew words designating possession and acquisition. That is why miqneh naturally shifts from the concrete sense (the animals themselves) to the abstract sense (the wealth they represent).
H4735.emploi: The word miqneh appears 64 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Genesis, Exodus, and the historical books — the accounts of pastoral life and transactions. It designates the flocks of the patriarchs (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob) and kings (David, Hezekiah), and also appears in the plagues of Egypt (Exodus 9) where God strikes Pharaoh's livestock. The word is used both for the entire livestock and for specific animals in the flock (sheep, goats, cattle, camels). In legal contexts (Exodus 34:19, Numbers 31), it is used to establish rights — the right of the firstborn, the taking of spoils. It is a word fundamentally linked to the notion of property, wealth, and means of livelihood.
H4735.portee: For the biblical reader, understanding the role of the flock illuminates how ancient peoples of the East measure wealth and God's blessing — not by gold or movable goods, but by life itself, embodied in the animals raised and from which one lives. When the Bible speaks of a patriarch or king's "numerous flocks," it indicates that God has blessed them abundantly. This reminds us that true wealth, according to the Bible, is what reproduces and sustains life — a lesson that extends well beyond ancient livestock raising.

sens: The action of buying, acquiring something in exchange for money
What has been bought, possession obtained through purchase
The price paid to obtain something
A property obtained legally through purchase and which becomes ownership
H4736.detail:
1. Acquisition is primarily the act of buying: paying money to obtain something. In Genesis 17:12, Abraham must circumcise "every male acquired for money" — referring to slaves he purchased from foreigners. This is the commercial action, the monetary exchange.
2. Acquisition then refers to what has been bought itself, the property that has become possession. When Abraham buys the field of Machpelah (Genesis 23:18), this field becomes his "property" — it is the acquisition, the acquired good that can then be transferred or used.
3. By extension, the word can refer to the price itself, the cost of the purchase. In Leviticus 25:16, it speaks of raising or lowering the "price" according to the number of years remaining before the jubilee: this is the sum paid for the transaction.
4. Finally, acquisition can mean a right of ownership legally gained through purchase. In Jeremiah 32:12, the prophet receives and keeps the "deed of acquisition" for the field: this document establishes and guarantees his legal possession of the purchased property.
H4736.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root קנה (qanah), which means "to buy, to acquire." The family also includes קוני (qoni, "one who buys, owner") and other forms. The starting image is that of exchange: giving money to receive a good that becomes one's own. This Hebrew word is common in the legal and commercial texts of the Bible, where ownership must be clearly established.
H4736.emploi: The word appears 13 times in the Old Testament, mainly in accounts of sales and property laws. In Genesis, it refers to slaves or goods purchased: Abraham circumcises his acquired slaves (17:12, 17:23). In Leviticus, it appears in the rules of the jubilee, which govern the resale of lands and regulate the calculation of the price (25:16, 25:51). In Jeremiah 32, the word takes on a symbolic dimension: the acquisition of the field of Hanamel by Jeremiah, before witnesses and notarized documents (32:11-12), expresses the prophet's trust in the restoration of Israel after exile. Acquisition is never a private and secret act: it requires witnesses, contracts, a public establishment of the right.
H4736.portee: This word reminds us that ownership in biblical thought only exists when publicly recognized and legally framed. It invites the reader to understand that possessing implies responsibilities, especially towards the poor and the foreigners, and that God Himself recognizes and protects these rights. Jeremiah's acquisition of the field during the siege of Jerusalem becomes a lesson of faith: what we legally acquire, even in the midst of chaos, has lasting value in the eyes of God.

sens: Levite of second rank under the reign of David
Keeper of the ark of the covenant
Temple musician playing the harp
H4737.detail:
1. Miknéja was a Levite, meaning a member of the tribe dedicated to temple service. He held the rank of second order, which means he had important responsibilities but did not hold the top position in the priestly hierarchy (1 Chronicles 15:18).
2. He was one of the designated porters to guard the ark of the covenant, the sacred chest containing the tablets of the law. This role was considered an honor and a major responsibility in Israelite worship.
3. Miknéja was also a musician: he played the eight-string harp and participated in leading the singing during religious celebrations at the temple of Jerusalem under David (1 Chronicles 15:21). His role was thus both cultic and musical.
H4737.origine: The name Miknéja literally means "possession of Jehovah" or "one whom Jehovah possesses." It is composed of two elements: "miqneh" (possession, property) and "Jah" (short form of the divine name). This name expresses that its bearer belongs to God and depends on His blessing, which was a common way for Hebrews to acknowledge divine authority over their lives.
H4737.emploi: Miknéja is mentioned twice in the Bible, both in 1 Chronicles, in the context of the solemn ceremony of the transfer of the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem under King David. First listed among the Levites of the second order responsible for guarding the ark (1 Chronicles 15:18), he reappears immediately after in the list of musicians playing the harp to lead the liturgical singing (1 Chronicles 15:21). These two mentions show that he held both religious and musical responsibilities, which was common for Levites at that time.

sens: Prediction or word given as coming from God
Divination or omen declared by occult means
False religious message presented as a divine revelation
H4738.detail:
1. An oracle is a word presented as coming directly from God, a prediction or divine message — what the false prophets of Israel claimed to receive and convey to the people (Ezekiel 13:7).
2. The word also refers more broadly to divination or omens obtained through occult practices, human methods to attempt to know the future or the divine will without God's authority.
3. In both verses from Ezekiel, God denounces the oracles as vain and deceptive: these false prophets utter lying words that they falsely attribute to the Lord (Ezekiel 12:24), thus fueling the people's illusion.
H4738.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to divide" or "to cut," evoking the idea of cutting through darkness to derive meaning or an omen. It is linked to pagan divination practices where one attempted to perceive the divine through human means — casting lots, observing signs, consulting spirits — methods strictly forbidden in the Mosaic Law.
H4738.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the prophet Ezekiel in the sixth century before Christ. In these two passages, God firmly condemns the false prophets and their deceptive oracles. Ezekiel 12:24 asserts that there will soon be no more such vain visions or lying oracles among Israel; Ezekiel 13:7 questions the false prophets about the vain and deceitful nature of their visions and oracles. The context is always that of divine judgment on religious falsehood.
H4738.portee: This word reminds the believer that only the true word of God, conveyed by His authentic prophets and recorded in the Scriptures, is worthy of trust. It warns against the seduction of false prophets who claim to speak in God's name, but whose words prove to be deceptive: it is a call to test every religious message in the light of God's authentic revelation.

sens: Locality in the territory of Israel during the time of the monarchy
H4739.detail: Makats is a city or region in the territory of Israel mentioned only once in the Bible, in the administrative context of King Solomon's kingdom. It appears in the list of districts providing for the king, where the son of Dekar was responsible for this locality as well as other nearby cities (Saalbim, Beth-Shemesh, Elon, and Beth-Hanan). Its exact location is uncertain, but it was likely situated in Judah or Benjamin, in the central region of the kingdom (1 Kings 4:9).
H4739.origine: The Hebrew name *maqats* is derived from a root that means "end" or "extremity." The name was borne by a particular place whose precise identity has been lost over time. No other character or place of this name appears elsewhere in the Scriptures.
H4739.emploi: Makats appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 4:9. This passage lists the twelve prefects established by King Solomon to administer the kingdom and gather royal provisions. Makats is included among several cities grouped under the authority of a single administrator, suggesting that it was a small urban center or a locality of minor administrative importance, although it was counted among the resources of the kingdom. Its precise geographical identity has not been established with certainty by modern archaeologists.

sens: fortified projection of a wall
corner or ridge of a structure
H4740G.detail:
1. The word refers to a defensive architectural structure: a projection or tower placed at the corner of a wall to strengthen the fortifications. In 2 Chronicles 26:9, King Uzziah builds towers "at the corner gate" of Jerusalem, meaning at those strategic points of the wall where it changes direction.
2. More broadly, the word evokes any corner or ridge of a structure, the part where two surfaces meet.
H4740G.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to cut" or "to slice," hence the idea of something forming a cutting edge, a ridge. This sense of "corner" or "angle" arises from the physical image of the meeting point where the wall sharply and abruptly changes direction. The masculine singular form allows for the precise designation of such a defensive structure.
H4740G.emploi: The word appears only once in the provided biblical text: in 2 Chronicles 26:9, where it describes an element of the fortifications of Jerusalem during the time of Uzziah (king of Judah). Its use is situated in a context of military architecture and city defense works. This passage shows that the kings of Judah invested in angular structures to secure their capital.
H4740G.portee: This word reminds us how God grants kings and peoples the talents to build, organize, and protect themselves. Uzziah's fortifications also testify to the prosperity and stability that God can bestow upon a faithful reign. For the Christian reader, this illustrates that divine providence manifests in the concrete details of human life, including construction and material security.

sens: place where two surfaces or lines meet sharply
protruding or reinforced part of a structure
strategic point of a fortification
H4740H.detail: 1. The word primarily designates the point where two walls or elements intersect or join: it is an angle in the geometric sense. In the plans of the Tabernacle in Exodus 26:24, the boards "at the two angles" are structural pieces that meet at the end. 2. It is also, more specifically, a projection or reinforcement: a piece of wood or stone that forms an angle to consolidate or mark an important corner. The repairs of the wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah 3:19-25 mention "the angle" several times, which is a key point of the fortification. 3. By extension, it is a fortified or strategic point of a wall, an angle tower: a vulnerable but crucial place, thus monitored and reinforced.
H4740H.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that conveys the idea of "to cut" or "to bevel," hence "to make a projection" or "to form an angle." This image of sharpness or projection characterizes the angular shape. The word is rare and technical; it primarily designates architectural elements.
H4740H.emploi: The word appears 9 times, always in contexts of construction or fortification. In Exodus 26 and 36 (description of the Tabernacle), it names the double boards at the "angles" that structure the building. In Nehemiah 3, during the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem, it becomes a topographical landmark: "the angle" is marked as a point where the wall changes direction or where it is particularly reinforced. In Ezekiel 41 and 46, the "angles" of the future Temple divide the space into distinct zones. The word remains always concrete and architectural.
H4740H.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible does not disdain technical and concrete details. Understanding the "angles" of the Tabernacle or the wall helps us visualize the text and respect its historical precision. It is also a sign that God reigns over the material details of His project: the construction of the Tabernacle, the reconstruction of Jerusalem, the organization of the future Temple are sacred acts where every joint, every angle matters.

sens: tool for scraping or shaping wood
instrument for marking or scratching
knife used for shaping idols
H4741.detail:
1. It is a scraping or shaping tool, used for scraping, digging, or smoothing wood and other materials. The unique example comes from Isaiah 44:13, where the craftsman uses it to shape a wooden statue intended to be an idol: he handles it after having drawn his design with a pencil and string.
2. The word evokes the action of scraping, removing shavings or chips, until the desired shape is obtained. It is a gesture of a sculptor or carpenter.
3. In the context of Isaiah's prophecy, this instrument becomes a symbol of the vain human work of making a false deity: an inert object that is carved to give it a divine appearance.
H4741.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to cut" or "to slice." It expresses the idea of separating, dividing, or removing a part. The term thus concretely designates the instrument that cuts, scrapes, or shapes — here, a knife or scraper used in woodworking.
H4741.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 44:13. It is used in a prophecy where Isaiah describes the absurd process of making a wooden idol: the carpenter-craftsman draws his plan with a pencil, then uses a knife to dig and shape the block. This context shows that the word designates a concrete tool of the woodworking trade, but the Bible uses it primarily to highlight the futility of idolatry.
H4741.portee: This word reminds us that idols are objects made by human hands, shaped by the sweat of the brow with ordinary tools. It underscores the absurdity of worshiping what human hands have created, which the prophet Isaiah develops by showing the contrast between the living God and the mute wooden deities. For the Christian reader, it is a call to recognize the futility of anything that claims to replace God.

sens: The corner or edge of a structure
An angular reinforcement of a construction
The junction of two surfaces that meet
H4742.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the corner or edge formed by the meeting of two structural elements — it is the point or line of angle in a construction. In the description of the tabernacle (Exodus 26:23), the text speaks of "boards for the angles of the tabernacle, at the back": these are the corner beams that reinforce the wooden structure of the sanctuary at the corners, particularly at the rear.
2. More specifically, it is an angular reinforcement or buttress, a piece of framing placed at the angle to consolidate the junction of two walls. The parallel in Exodus 36:28 confirms this structural function in the actual construction of the tabernacle.
H4742.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of "to cut," "to reduce," or "to shape," suggesting something cut or shaped with precision. The form of the word indicates a structure or piece molded to occupy a specific place or function — here, the angle. It is a concrete term of carpentry and architecture.
H4742.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, solely in the descriptions of the tabernacle in Exodus 26 and 36. These two passages are parallel: they describe the construction of the sacred dwelling, a work of meticulous craftsmanship according to the plans given by God to Moses. The context is that of wooden materials (acacia) intended to form the enclosure of the sanctuary. The corner boards mentioned are key elements of architectural strength and balance, placed "at the back," that is, at the rear of the building.
H4742.portee: This word reminds us that the presence of God among His people rests on a real construction, thought out in its details. The reinforcing angles evoke meticulous solidity and stability: the House of God is not a fragile edifice, but built with wisdom and strength. For the believer, this speaks of the reliability and justice of God.

sens: Physical decomposition of living flesh, of a wound that becomes infected
Progressive degeneration of the body due to illness or divine punishment
Extreme weakness, languor, withering of the whole being
Figuratively: moral and spiritual corruption
H4743.detail:
1. The word primarily describes concrete decay: flesh that disintegrates, putrefies. In Zechariah 14:12, during an apocalyptic plague, the flesh of the enemies falls into decay while they are still standing, their eyes and tongue consumed by decay — a horrific image of living destruction.
2. It also applies to infected wounds that suppurate and necrose. The psalmist in Psalms 38:6 cries: "My wounds are infected and festering," showing how the decay of a wound can express spiritual suffering.
3. Often the word loses its rawness to become languor, a slow consumption: in Leviticus 26:39 and Ezekiel 4:17, the survivors are struck with languor, meaning they gradually weaken, eaten away from within by divine punishment.
4. In a deeper sense, this decay of the body symbolizes a decay of the soul: in Ezekiel 33:10, the people recognize that under the weight of their sins, they are struck with languor, meaning their transgression is rotting them from the inside.
H4743.origine: The Hebrew root māqaq evokes the idea of dissolution, melting: something that weakens, flows, crumbles. It belongs to a family of words expressing progressive destruction (to rot, to melt, to dissolve). The basic image is that of living flesh degrading, losing its cohesion, becoming infected. It is a raw, concrete word that easily borrows from the realm of disease to speak of divine punishment.
H4743.emploi: The word appears 7 times in biblical Hebrew, concentrated in the prophets. Leviticus 26:39 uses it as a threat of the covenant: the survivors will be struck with languor for their sins. In Ezekiel (four passages), it is a theme of punishment: the exiled people languish under their iniquity (4:17, 24:23, 33:10) — not just physical suffering, but a sign of progressive divine punishment. In Psalms 38:6, it is a confession: my wounds are festering, an expression of my guilt. Zechariah 14:12 reserves it for the ultimate judgment: a miraculous plague where the flesh of the enemies of Jerusalem rots while standing. The meaning nuances: first physical decay, then languor (chronic weakening), then a metaphor for punishment.
H4743.portee: This word shows that the Bible expresses divine punishment not as a sudden explosion, but as a slow corruption, a consumption that gnaws at the being from within. It is a call to take seriously the hidden consequence of sin: not only guilt, but existential weakening. At the same time, it makes illness and languor possible signs of divine action — which helps the believer discern the spiritual meaning of their suffering and turn towards repentance.

sens: Action of calling, of summoning the people to gather
Sacred assembly, gathering called by God for a day of feast
Set day for this sacred gathering
Act of reading or proclaiming
H4744.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the action of calling or summoning: it is what gathers people, like the sound of silver trumpets that summons the assembly of Israel in the wilderness (Numbers 10:2).
2. In Israel's worship, a convocation is a sacred gathering ordained by God during the major feasts: Passover, Pentecost, Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, Tabernacles (Leviticus 23:4, 21). It is a day when the people gather to honor the Lord.
3. By extension, the word also designates the day itself when this sacred gathering takes place — a day of rest, when no one works (Exodus 12:16).
4. Rarely, it can also mean the act of reading or publicly proclaiming, as in Nehemiah 8:8 where the Law is read to the assembly.
H4744.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root "qr" which means "to call" or "to cry out." The prefix "m" ("mi") forms a noun designating the action itself. This root is found in "qol" (voice, cry) and in the verb "qara" (to call). Literally, a "miqra" is therefore "a call" — that which gathers people by a cry or call.
H4744.emploi: The word appears 23 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the books of the Law (Leviticus and Numbers) and in Nehemiah. It always designates a sacred gathering prescribed by God. Leviticus 23 enumerates it for each feast of the religious calendar: it is a fixed formula to mark the days when God wants to gather His people. These convocations are "holy" and involve a prohibition of servile work. Isaiah 1:13 shows that these convocations, devoid of sincerity, become burdensome in the eyes of God. In Nehemiah 8:8, the term takes on nuance by meaning the proclaimed reading of the Law to the gathered people.
H4744.portee: This word reminds Christians that God calls His people to gather, not by administrative constraint but by a sacred convocation where He wants to meet His own. The feast convocations structured the life of Israel around the relationship with the God of the covenant. For today, this speaks to the importance of the common gathering of believers to worship and listen to the Word, not out of dead obligation but as a living response to God's call.

sens: Encounter or unexpected event, which seems to occur without cause or intention
Fortuitous circumstance that escapes will or control
Fate or common condition that happens to all without distinction
Lot or end that awaits a person or creature
H4745.detail:
1. An encounter or event that occurs without being sought or anticipated: Ruth goes to glean and "it happened by chance that the piece of land belonged to Boaz" (Ruth 2:3) — she did not know that this field was his, but this "coincidence" changes her entire destiny.

2. A misfortune or calamity that strikes without knowing where it comes from: the Philistines ask God to prove that the plague afflicting them truly comes from Him, "otherwise, we will know that it is not His hand that has struck us, but that it has happened to us by chance" (1 Samuel 6:9) — in other words, by an ordinary cause, not divine.

3. The condition or fate that happens to each person, regardless of their will or wisdom: Ecclesiastes observes that "the wise and the foolish have the same fate," that they both die (Ecclesiastes 2:14-15) — death is the same for all, rich or poor, wise or foolish.
H4745.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to meet" or "to happen." It designates what presents itself before someone without them having anticipated or caused it — a fortuitous encounter. It is the word that the Bible uses to speak of what seems to escape control: apparent chance, the fate that befalls all.
H4745.emploi: This word appears about 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the books of Ruth, 1 Samuel, and especially Ecclesiastes. In Ruth, it designates the providential "coincidence" of Ruth gleaning in Boaz's field — an encounter that seems fortuitous but bears fruit. In 1 Samuel, it speaks of an event that cannot be attributed to the direct action of God, hence the challenge from the Philistines. In Ecclesiastes, the wise man uses it to express his doubt: is everything just vanity and chance? The wise and the foolish, human and beast, all have the same fate — death — which raises the question of the meaning of life. It is a pessimistic, philosophical word that conveys human uncertainty in the face of events.
H4745.portee: This word challenges the believer on the tension between God's providence and what appears accidental. In Ruth, the "chance" that seems pure turns out to be God's guiding action. But Ecclesiastes uses it to express doubt: if everything seems chance and vanity, where is the meaning? It is an invitation not to rely on appearances, but to seek how God acts even through what seems fortuitous.

sens: set of beams and wooden pieces that form the structure of a roof
by extension, structure of a building
state of dilapidation of a house
H4746.detail: 1. The word refers to the wooden beams and load-bearing elements of a roof or house. It is the solid structure that supports the building and protects it. In Ecclesiastes 10:18, when hands are lazy, the framework "collapses": the image is that of a poorly maintained house whose beams weaken and gradually fall apart. 2. Figuratively, the word applies to the entire building and its general state of maintenance. When the framework weakens, the whole building deteriorates: leaks appear, gutters form. It is the biblical image of negligence and laziness: what is not cared for naturally collapses.
H4746.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of meeting or coincidence — here, the way the wooden beams meet and assemble to form the roof structure. It is a concrete and technical term used to describe the ancient architecture of Jewish houses, where the roof was made of wooden beams covered with earth or vegetation.
H4746.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ecclesiastes 10:18. It is used in a teaching about the consequences of laziness. The wise man uses the image of a house whose framework collapses to show how inaction and negligence lead to ruin. It is a technical and concrete word, chosen to make the teaching vivid and striking: everyone understands that a poorly maintained house eventually collapses.
H4746.portee: This passage teaches us that laziness has concrete and visible consequences. Like a house whose framework gradually collapses, our life — our family, our work, our faith — deteriorates progressively if we do not maintain it with vigilance. It is a call to diligence and responsibility for what God entrusts to us.

sens: Quality of what is fresh, absence of heat
H4747.detail: 1. The word properly refers to freshness or the coolness of a place — the quality of being fresh, pleasant due to the absence of excessive heat. It is in summer, when it is very hot, that one particularly appreciates the freshness of a well-ventilated room or a shaded spot. In Judges 3:20, Ehud goes to see King Eglon in his "upper chamber" which enjoyed this freshness; the word emphasizes the intimacy and comfort of the place. In Judges 3:24, the same word reappears to describe this freshness sought in a secluded place away from the oppressive sun of the Middle East.
H4747.origine: The Hebrew word מְקֵרָה (meqerah) comes from a root meaning "to be fresh" or "to cool down." It is formed from the verb קרר (qarar), which literally evokes the action of cooling or making fresh. The root itself suggests a contrast with heat: it is the idea of finding rest and relaxation away from the scorching desert sun.
H4747.emploi: This word appears twice in the Bible, both in Judges 3, during the account where Ehud kills the Moabite king Eglon. In both occurrences (verses 20 and 24), it refers to an upper chamber, a place of freshness and rest. This chamber was a private and comfortable place, hence its importance in the narrative: it is a secluded place where Ehud can be alone with the king. The use of the term emphasizes the comfort and intimacy of this space, key elements for understanding how Ehud was able to accomplish his act of deliverance.
H4747.portee: The word "freshness" reminds us that the material details of daily life — seeking freshness, finding rest — are part of the biblical universe. It is a simple word that makes the narrative human and vivid: even an important act of deliverance takes place in concrete places, with real bodily needs.

sens: Carefully arranged hair, elaborate hairstyle
Refined hair adornment, sign of dignity and beauty
External mark of well-being and prosperity
H4748.detail:
1. The word refers to a worked and well-arranged hairstyle, probably curly or wavy, as was prepared among wealthy women. It is a work of hair artistry, the result of meticulous care. In Isaiah 3:24, these elegant curly hairs contrast with the bald head of the exiled woman: it is the image of lost feminine beauty.
2. This hairstyle more broadly represents dignity, femininity in beauty, and belonging to a wealthy social class. Only women who could afford it could have their hair styled in this way.
3. In the passage from Isaiah, the curly hair symbolizes prosperity, well-being, and grace before judgment: the prophet lists all the ornaments that the women of Jerusalem will lose — perfume, belt, elegant hairstyle, mantle — all signs that God will remove as punishment.
H4748.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root evoking the work of the turner, the artisan who shapes with art. The word reinforces the idea that this hairstyle is not natural, but the result of work, of a deliberate shaping. This is why ancient translations speak of "turned work" or "artwork" applied to hair.
H4748.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 3:24. It is part of the series of misfortunes that the prophet enumerates: instead of perfume, an infection; instead of the belt, a rope; instead of this beautiful hairstyle, a bald head. This context shows that the word designates an element of feminine beauty, an ornament of social status that divine judgment will take away from the proud women of Jerusalem.
H4748.portee: This word reminds us that true beauty and human dignity do not reside in external adornments or social status, but in what God values. By listing all that will be lost, Isaiah encourages the reader not to set their heart on passing appearances, but on a right relationship with God.

sens: work of gold or silver shaped by hammering, forming a unique piece
finely crafted cult object, of great value and beauty
H4749.detail:
1. The word literally refers to gold or silver that has been struck and re-struck with a hammer to give it its final shape. It is a precise artisanal work where the goldsmith shapes the metal into a single coherent piece, without seams. The two golden cherubim of the mercy seat (Exodus 25:18) and the lampstand of the sanctuary (Exodus 25:31) are both described as made of "beaten gold," which emphasizes the perfection and unity of the piece.
2. Beyond the technique, the term evokes the precious and sacred quality of these objects. An object of "beaten gold" is not ordinary: it is a work of great value, worthy of being in the sanctuary of God, crafted with care and respect. This reflects the splendor and dignity appropriate for the worship of the Lord.
H4749.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to strike" or "to beat." The "beaten gold" is literally the gold that has been hammered, a mark of the meticulous craftsmanship and skill of the goldsmith. This image of hammering evokes effort, precision, and the transformation of raw metal into a work of art.
H4749.emploi: The term appears only in a few passages of Exodus and Numbers (8 occurrences), always to describe the objects of the sanctuary. It applies to the golden cherubim of the mercy seat (Exodus 25:18; 37:7), to the pure gold lampstand (Exodus 25:31; 37:17), and to its branches (Exodus 25:36; 37:22). It is also used for the silver trumpets that Moses is to have made (Numbers 10:2). Each time, the context emphasizes the uniqueness of the piece: "of one piece." It is the preferred vocabulary for designating the masterpieces of sacred furniture.
H4749.portee: This word reveals how God desires His worship to be celebrated with excellence and beauty. The objects of the sanctuary are not ordinary, but crafted with care, in a way that reflects the holiness and majesty of God. For the believer, this reminds us that serving God deserves our best: not out of pride, but out of reverence and gratitude.

sens: A place planted with cucumbers, usually a small structure or temporary shelter to keep the harvest
A massive and immobile structure, incapable of action
An inert and useless thing
H4750.detail:
1. A cucumber field literally refers to a place where this vegetable grows, often with a small hut or shelter to watch over and protect the harvest. In Isaiah 1:8, Jerusalem after God's judgment is compared to "a hut in a cucumber field" — that is, abandoned, solitary, and defenseless, like those precarious shelters seen alone amidst the crops.
2. The word also denotes a massive and solid structure but completely frozen, incapable of moving or acting. In Jeremiah 10:5, idols are said to be "massive" like columns: they have an imposing shape, but they are immobile, silent, and powerless.
3. By extension, the word evokes what is inert, sterile, lifeless, or of no real utility — a biting critique of false gods that claim power but are empty of substance.
H4750.origine: The Hebrew word miq.shah comes from the root q.š.h which means "to harden" or "to become hard." The word originally designates what is solid, compact, massive — hence the image of the small structure built in a cucumber field, a simple but robust construction. The biblical image plays on the isolation and precariousness of this type of temporary shelter in a rural setting.
H4750.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible. In Isaiah 1:8, it illustrates the contrast between Jerusalem's past majesty and its present desolation after invasions — the capital is reduced to a solitary hut in the fields. In Jeremiah 10:5, the same word takes on an ironic nuance: the idols of the nations are massive like columns, but inert, without speech or power. In both cases, the word emphasizes inefficacy, isolation, or abandonment.
H4750.portee: This word invites the reader to see beyond imposing appearances. Idols may seem solid and important, but they are as empty as an abandoned hut in a field. For the believer, it is a call not to be impressed by what appears great or powerful if it is devoid of the presence and action of the true God.

sens: Having an unpleasant, sour, or pungent taste
Causing physical or moral suffering
Expressing pain, regret, or anger
Filling with sadness or disappointment
Discontented, irritated, furious
H4751.detail:
1. It is primarily a quality of taste: a bitter drink or food is unpleasant to drink or eat. In Exodus 15:23, the waters that Moses finds in the desert are bitter and undrinkable. This is concrete and sensory.

2. By extension, the word denotes suffering itself, particularly moral pain and anguish. Job speaks of his bitterness when he suffers (Job 7:11): he laments his afflicted soul, as one might say "in the bitterness of my heart."

3. The word also describes the feeling that accompanies this suffering: regret, sorrow, lamentation. Esau cries out with bitterness when he discovers he has lost his blessing (Genesis 27:34); it is the cry of a man who deeply regrets and suffers.

4. It can finally express irritation, anger, or a difficult mood. In 1 Samuel 22:2, David gathers around him all the discontented, those who are bitter, embittered by their circumstances; they are furious about their situation.

5. The word also applies to what causes suffering or disappointment: the end of the prostitute is bitter (Proverbs 5:4), meaning painful and regrettable.
H4751.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to be acrid or harsh in taste." It primarily designates an unpleasant physical sensation, then extends to anything that is painful, difficult, or causes sorrow. This progression from the sensory to the spiritual is typical of Hebrew: the body helps express the states of the soul. The word also appears as a noun (bitterness) and as an adverb (bitterly, with sorrow).
H4751.emploi: The word appears about 34 times in the Old Testament, mainly in poetry and accounts of distress. Alongside metaphors of water (bitter waters of the desert, waters of cursing from the suspected woman test), it is used to express strong emotions related to suffering: sorrow (Genesis 27:34), anguish (Job 7:11), irritation (1 Samuel 22:2). Isaiah uses it to describe affliction due to illness (38:15). In Proverbs, bitterness is the final result of poor choices (5:4, 27:7). The meaning slightly changes depending on the context: sometimes it is a sensation, sometimes an emotion, sometimes a character or mood, but always with the idea of an unpleasant and painful experience.
H4751.portee: This word reminds the reader that life experiences true suffering, whether physical or moral, and that the Bible does not minimize this experience. It names it frankly. But at the same time, it shows that bitterness often has a cause and a lesson: it can be the fruit of our choices (Proverbs), or a trial that awakens us to the fragility of our earthly consolations. Recognizing bitterness is a step toward spiritual honesty and sometimes toward repentance or turning to God.

sens: a small portion of liquid that falls or flows
figuratively, an infinitesimal, negligible quantity
H4752.detail:
1. A drop is a very small quantity of liquid, one that falls drop by drop or flows slowly from a source. It is the image of a regular and small flow, particle by particle.
2. Figuratively, the drop represents the infinitesimal, the insignificant: in Isaiah 40:15, the most powerful nations are "like a drop from a bucket" compared to God. They are so small that they weigh nothing on the cosmic scale. It is a striking way of saying that everything that seems great in human eyes becomes dust before the majesty of God.
H4752.origine: The Hebrew word מַר (mar) comes from a root meaning "to flow" or "to run." What flows regularly and drop by drop defines the basic image. The word belongs to the family of verbs of flow and outflow.
H4752.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 40:15, where the prophet uses it to express the humiliation of nations before God. In this context of consolation addressed to the exiles, the prophet reminds that all earthly power is reduced to an insignificant drop of water. The poetic image emphasizes the dizzying contrast between the greatness of God and the smallness of creation.
H4752.portee: This word highlights a fundamental truth for the believer: the realities that impress and terrify us here on earth — political powers, wealth, threats — are actually infinitesimal before God. This invites the Christian to put his fears and earthly ambitions into perspective and to place his trust in the One who holds everything in His hand.

sens: Aromatic resin extracted from a tree in Arabia
Perfume or fragrant substance used in cosmetics and personal care
Offering or luxury gift
Image of beauty, delicacy, or love
H4753.detail:
1. Myrrh is a precious resin that flows naturally from the bark of an Arabian tree: it is a rare and costly product, highly valued in antiquity. In Exodus 30:23, it is part of the composition of the holy anointing oil used in worship, alongside cinnamon and fragrant cane, which shows its sacred character and great value.

2. It is used to perfume the body and clothing: it is a luxury cosmetic sought after by women of high rank. In Esther 2:12, young women spend six months beautifying themselves with myrrh oil before meeting the king, demonstrating that it is a prestigious beautifying product.

3. It is used to scent clothing and places, creating an atmosphere of refinement and nobility. In Psalm 45:9, myrrh, aloes, and cassia perfume all the garments of the king, symbols of his royal magnificence.

4. It becomes a poetic image of beauty, tenderness, and love. In Song of Solomon 1:13, the beloved is compared to "a bundle of myrrh," expressing the allure and sweetness of his presence; in 3:6, the beloved is seen coming up from the wilderness "with fragrant myrrh," creating an atmosphere of intimacy and desire.
H4753.origine: The Hebrew word mor refers to myrrh, a precious gum-resin. Its primary image is that of a substance that "flows" or "exudes" from the tree, hence its etymological link to the idea of fluidity. In Greek, this word is translated as σμύρνα (smyrna), a term that has given rise to proper names and other derivatives in modern languages. Myrrh was one of the three gifts brought by the Magi to the child Jesus (Matthew 2:11), symbolizing his dignity and foreshadowing his Passion.
H4753.emploi: The word mor appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in poetic and legislative texts. It first appears in the worship prescriptions (Exodus 30:23) as a component of the holy anointing oil reserved for the priests and the tabernacle. It also appears in historical narratives: in Esther 2:12, it is a prestigious cosmetic product. But it is especially in biblical poetry that myrrh becomes symbolic: Psalm 45 associates it with royalty and splendor, while the Song of Solomon (1:13, 3:6, 4:6, 4:14, 5:1, 5:5, 5:13) uses it to express the beauty of the beloved's body and the sweetness of love. Its use in the Song of Solomon reveals how a precious and rare substance becomes a metaphor for intimate and delicate love.
H4753.portee: Myrrh reminds the reader that God surrounds his worship with what is beautiful, precious, and fragrant: it elevates the heart towards the dignity of meeting with God. In the Song of Solomon, it invites the believer to discover beauty, tenderness, and legitimate desire in human love, reflecting divine love. It also speaks of intimacy: myrrh perfumes what is close to the heart (the garment, the bed, the beloved body), suggesting that beauty and love touch our senses and emotions in a profound and sensitive way.

sens: Rapid movement, the rush of an animal charging forward
Agitation, turbulence, untamed character
Rebellion, refusal to submit to authority
H4754.detail:
1. In Job 39:21, the word describes the impetuous rush of the horse when it rises: it is this vigorous movement, this kind of charge that characterizes the spirited animal, untamed by nature.
2. The meaning extends to any form of agitation or turbulence: the word evokes less a deliberate act than raw vigor, an unbridled energy that cannot be contained.
3. In Zephaniah 3:1, "rebellious city" designates a city that refuses order, discipline, authority — a city characterized by this same untamed nature, this refusal to submit that recalls the agitation of the wild horse.
H4754.origine: The Hebrew word, from a root not certainly known, is linked to the idea of violent movement and agitation. Its use in these two contexts (the horse, the city) suggests a primary image of turbulence or spirit: it is raw agitation, movement that escapes control. The duality of meanings (physical agitation of the horse, then moral insubordination of the city) reveals how Hebrew often uses images from the animal world to speak of human behavior.
H4754.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Job 39:21, it describes the war horse at the moment it takes its charge, an image of power and animal spirit. In Zephaniah 3:1, it qualifies Jerusalem itself as a "rebellious city" — the same energy that makes the horse great becomes here a sign of a city's insubordination to God. Both uses play on this tension: the term can evoke admiration (the natural spirit of the horse) or condemnation (the culpable untamed nature of a city that refuses to repent).
H4754.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize where true rebellion lies: not primarily in isolated acts, but in this inner agitation, this spirit that refuses to accept the restraint of wisdom and the authority of God. Like the horse that charges forward without listening to its rider, the city that surrenders to the "race" of its passions is lost. It is a lesson on the importance of the submission of the soul, not to break human vitality, but to direct it towards good.

sens: Name given to Naomi when she returns to Bethlehem after mourning
Literally means "bitterness"
H4755.detail:
1. Mara is the name that Naomi gives herself upon returning to Bethlehem, stripped of her husband and two sons, all dead during the famine in Moab. She says: "Call me Mara, for the Almighty has made my life very bitter" (Ruth 1:20). This is an act of renaming that expresses her despair: she rejects her former happy name to define herself by her pain.
2. The word literally means "bitterness" — not a bitterness of taste, but that of a heart crushed by misfortune. Naomi believes that God himself has filled her with sorrow, and she bears the weight of this by changing her identity. This is not merely a figure of speech: it is a woman who now sees herself as marked by tragedy.
H4755.origine: The Hebrew word mara (מָרָא) means "bitterness." It comes from the root that expresses the idea of a bitter substance, often in Hebrew associated with moral pain as much as with physical taste. This is not a name given to Naomi at birth, but a nickname she applies to herself as a sign of mourning — a way of saying: "I have become another woman, marked by suffering."
H4755.emploi: Naomi appears only once under this name in Ruth 1:20, at the moment of her return to Bethlehem. She asks the women of the city to call her Mara instead of Naomi (which means "pleasantness" or "delight"). This is a decisive moment: she rejects the identity of a blessed woman for that of a burdened woman. This renaming marks her refusal to pretend to happiness while she feels abandoned. Yet, the rest of the book of Ruth will show that the Lord has not forgotten her: she will be comforted by her grandson Obed, an ancestor of King David.
H4755.portee: This moment of distress and renaming teaches every reader that it is permissible to cry out one's pain before God, without a mask — Naomi does not force herself to smile. But it also reminds us that our current sufferings are never the final word from God: the book of Ruth shows us how faithfulness and grace transform bitterness into comfort and blessing.

sens: One who exercises authority over others, particularly a king
God, as the one who sovereignly reigns over all
H4756.detail:
1. The word designates one who commands and to whom one obeys — notably a king. It is a title of respect and submission. Daniel uses it when addressing the king of Babylon: "My lord, let the dream be for your enemies" (Daniel 4:19), thus acknowledging royal authority over him.
2. It also applies to God, who reigns over all and everyone. When Daniel asserts that the God of Israel is "the Lord of kings" (Daniel 2:47), he proclaims that God surpasses all earthly sovereigns and possesses absolute authority. In chapter 5:23, the prophet reminds the king that he has not glorified "the God who holds your breath in His hand," showing that God alone is truly master of life and destiny.
H4756.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of dominating, commanding. It is closely related to other Hebrew terms denoting authority and power. Its fundamental meaning is one of superiority in strength and power — hence the title given to a king or to God.
H4756.emploi: This word appears only four times in the New Testament — all occurrences are in the book of Daniel, at the time when Daniel interprets the dreams of the king of Babylon. Daniel uses it as a title of respect towards the king (Daniel 4:19 and 4:24), but also to affirm God's superiority over the kings of this world (Daniel 2:47 and 5:23). It is a word from late Aramaic, used in a context of exile where the Jews must recognize the political authority of pagan kings while proclaiming the ultimate sovereignty of their God.
H4756.portee: This word reminds the reader that there are two kinds of lords: human authorities, whose temporal power can be acknowledged, and God alone, whose lordship is absolute and eternal. It invites discernment about where to place true loyalty and to remember that even the kings of the world are subject to the one who "holds in His hand" the life of each person.

sens: king of Babylon during the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah
H4757.detail: Merodach-Baladan is the king of Babylon who sends an embassy to Hezekiah to congratulate him on his healing. He reigns during the time of the Divided Monarchy, when Judah is still an independent kingdom alongside Israel. His gesture shows the interest that foreign powers had in the affairs of Judah.
H4757.origine: The name means "Marduk has given a son." Marduk was the chief god of Babylon, and the king bears this theophoric name to affirm his religious legitimacy. It is a typical compound name of Mesopotamian kings, which associates the name of a deity with a formula of blessing or filiation.
H4757.emploi: Merodach-Baladan is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 39:1, where he sends a letter and a gift to Hezekiah after learning of his illness and miraculous healing. He is also cited in 2 Kings 20:12, in the same context. He is a historical figure, king of Babylon in the 8th century BC, whose passage shows that he recognized the political and religious importance of the king of Judah.

sens: What the eyes see of a person or thing, its physical appearance
The impression or spectacle that something gives at first glance
The way something presents itself, its visible state
A supernatural vision, a divine appearance
The ability to see, sight
H4758.detail:
1. What the eyes see of a person or thing: physical appearance, silhouette, the form that catches the eye. For example, in Genesis 29:17, Leah "had tender eyes, but Rachel was beautiful in form" — her beauty was visible in her aspect. However, "the Lord looks at the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7), for deceptive appearance reveals nothing of true worth.
2. The impression or spectacle that something gives at first glance, what is offered to the gaze. In Leviticus 13:4, the priest examines a spot: "if there is a white spot that does not appear deeper than the skin," he evaluates its aspect to decide on leprosy. In Job 40:28, the mere aspect of Behemoth "is one not overwhelmed?"
3. The way something presents itself, its visible state or general condition. In Deuteronomy 28:67, the man in anguish says "in the presence" (in view) of what his eyes will see — it is the aspect of reality that terrifies.
4. A supernatural vision, a divine appearance intended for the one who receives it. Ezekiel 1:28 describes the aspect of the glory of the Lord as a rainbow: "At this sight, I fell on my face" — the prophetic vision overwhelms him. These appearances are never ordinary; they reveal the presence and power of God.
5. The ability to see, sight itself, and by extension direct perception. In Exodus 3:3, Moses says: "I will turn aside to see this great sight" — the aspect of this bush is so extraordinary that it draws attention.
H4758.origine: The Hebrew word mareh comes from a root that means "to see, to look" (the same that gives ראה raah). Literally, mareh designates what is "visible," what is offered to the view. It describes both ordinary appearance (the beauty of a woman, the state of a wound) and the supernatural image (the vision received by a prophet). This term emphasizes the importance of sight and what can be directly perceived by the eyes.
H4758.emploi: This word appears 82 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Ezekiel (which has 23 occurrences in his prophetic visions), in Genesis, in Leviticus, and in Daniel. It covers very diverse contexts: the physical appearance of people (Genesis 24:16, "Rebekah was beautiful in form"), the medical examination of wounds (Leviticus 13, where the word appears more than 10 times), the aspect of the temple and its architectural details (Ezekiel 40-43), and especially divine visions (Ezekiel 1:28, Daniel 8:15). In visions, the word marks that the prophet sees a reality that surpasses ordinary appearances: the aspect of divine glory is incomparable and provokes a physical reaction (fear, prostration). The meaning shifts from the observable to the supernatural depending on the context.
H4758.portee: This word reminds the reader that external appearance — beauty, strength, presence — reveals nothing of a person's true worth or what God sees in them. At the same time, the supernatural visions in which the word mareh appears show that God can make Himself visible in an overwhelming way: seeing the aspect of His glory transforms the one who receives it. That is why God says to Samuel: "The Lord does not look at what man looks at; man looks at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart."

sens: Supernatural appearance through which God reveals Himself to a prophet
Divine manifestation perceived internally, different from a dream
Ordinary way in which God communicates His will to prophets
H4759A.detail:
1. A vision is a supernatural appearance or revelation through which God shows Himself and speaks directly to a prophet. It is as if heaven opens before the eyes of man: Ezekiel says, "the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God" (Ezekiel 1:1). Samuel receives a vision at night where God calls him by name (1 Samuel 3:15).
2. A vision can occur in a state of trance or spiritual elevation: the person remains conscious but sees scenes transported before him, far from his body. Ezekiel is seized "between heaven and earth" and "transported, in visions of God, to Jerusalem" to behold the abominations of the temple (Ezekiel 8:3).
3. The vision is distinct from a dream: God says, "When there is a prophet among you, I, the Lord, will make Myself known to him in a vision; I will speak with him in a dream" (Numbers 12:6). The vision is a more direct and certain form of divine revelation.
H4759A.origine: The Hebrew word מַרְאָה comes from the root ראה (see), which literally means "that which is seen" or "that which appears." It is thus a vision in the sense of an appearance, a spectacle revealed to the eyes. The word is related to the ordinary term for sight or appearance. For a prophet, a vision is not a mere hallucination: it is a real manifestation of God that opens the inner or spiritual eyes of the seer.
H4759A.emploi: This word appears 10 times in the Old Testament, especially among the major prophets. Genesis 46:2 shows a nighttime vision of Jacob, where God speaks directly to him. Visions are the characteristic mode of revelation for prophets: Numbers 12:6 explicitly affirms this. Samuel (1 Samuel 3:15), Ezekiel (Ezekiel 1:1, 8:3, 40:2, 43:3), and Daniel (Daniel 10:7, 10:8, 10:16) all receive them. Ezekiel's visions are particularly spectacular and detailed: heavenly throne, extent of the walls of the future temple, glory of the Lord. Daniel also sees visions that terrify him. The word is always associated with the sacred: "visions of God" or "divine visions."
H4759A.portee: Understanding that the vision is a gift from the living God: it is His way of making direct contact with His prophets and entrusting them with His plans. For the biblical reader, visions show that God has not withdrawn from the world, but that He acts, speaks, and guides His people. They remind us that the supernatural reality exists and that God can open a man's eyes to show him what is hidden from others.

sens: Reflective object that returns an image
Symbol of what manifests reality
What allows one to see oneself
H4759B.detail:
1. A mirror is a polished metal object (here made of bronze) that reflects light and returns the image of the one looking at it. In Exodus 38:8, the women of Israel gave their mirrors so that Moses could melt them down and make the basin used for washing in the Tabernacle: these everyday objects, meant to reflect appearance, are transformed into a utensil for purification.
2. In the Bible and biblical thought, the mirror symbolizes what reveals reality — here, what shows what is, without falsehood. By giving their mirrors, the women confessed that all beauty and reality belong to God and can be consecrated to His service.
H4759B.origine: The Hebrew word מַרְאָה (mar'ah) comes from the root ראה (ra'ah), which means "to see." A mirror is thus literally "that which makes one see" or "that by which one sees." This etymology reveals the primary function of the object: it allows one to see, perceive, contemplate — first oneself, but also symbolically the truth.
H4759B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Exodus 38:8. This passage reports that the pious women who served at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting voluntarily gave their bronze mirrors. Moses melted these mirrors to extract the bronze and make the basin (or laver) intended for washing — a sacred utensil of worship. This act of consecration shows that even the most intimate and personal objects can be offered for God's service.
H4759B.portee: The mirror teaches us that our possessions — our goods, our talents, our appearance — only belong to us in use. The women of Israel understood that giving their mirrors to the Tabernacle was an act of worship: transforming the ordinary into the sacred. For us, this passage reminds us that everything we have can be offered to God, and that it is in sincere giving that it takes on its true value.

sens: Throat pouch in birds where food accumulates before digestion
Part of the bird that must be removed during the preparation of the sacrifice
H4760.detail:
1. The jabot is the muscular and membranous pouch located at the base of a bird's neck, between the esophagus and the stomach. It is where the bird stores and softens food before it descends into the digestive system. This organ often contains feathers, debris, and remnants of food that the bird has swallowed.
2. In Israelite worship, when a bird was offered as a sacrifice to God, the law required that the jabot with its feathers be removed and thrown onto the ash heap, east of the altar (Leviticus 1:16). It was the only organ specifically designated to be discarded: the rest of the bird was to be completely burned. This prescription made the bird pure and clean for the sacrifice.
H4760.origine: The Hebrew word מֻרְאָה (mur'ah) comes from a root that describes the action of regurgitating or expelling. The word literally designates what is excreted or expelled. In biblical Hebrew, this term is specific to birds and their digestive system, which is why it applies only to them.
H4760.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Leviticus 1:16. It is a precise cultic prescription: when offering a bird at the altar's ashes, the jabot had to be removed. This meticulousness reveals the Law's attention to the purity of the sacrifice and the respect for what is offered to God. It is a technical term of sacrificial language.
H4760.portee: This instruction shows that worship rendered to God requires purity and attention to detail. By rejecting the jabot with its impurities, one acknowledges that only what is pure and worthy can approach God. For the believer, this suggests that giving to God requires removing from oneself what defiles and offering sincerely what is genuine.

sens: The top of the human body, seat of intellect and authority
Position of chief, command, or preeminence
H4761.detail:
1. The word properly designates the head, the upper part of the body. In the text of Jeremiah 13:18, the fallen diadem "from your heads" is the royal ornament that rested on the head of the king and queen, making them symbols of power and dignity.
2. Figuratively, the "head" represents the function of chief or command. A king sitting at the head means he reigns and governs; losing one's head means losing authority. The image of the head bearing the diadem shows that the one who commands is placed above others, just as the head is above the body.
H4761.origine: The Hebrew word מְרַאֲשָׁוֹת (merashaoù) is formed from the root רֹאשׁ (rosh), which literally means "head." This root is fundamental in Hebrew: it first designates the physical organ, then by extension everything that is at the beginning, above, or in the first rank. The word can also be used as an adverb or preposition to indicate a position of precedence.
H4761.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jeremiah 13:18. There, it describes the diadem that falls from the head of the king and queen — a symbolic event of the loss of power and royal dignity. The context is that of God's judgment on Judah: the king and queen are stripped of their ornaments and authority. The image of the crown falling from the head illustrates the complete humiliation that befalls the land.
H4761.portee: This passage reminds us that earthly power is fragile and that only God holds the crowns and kingdoms. For the Christian reader, the fall of the diadem is a warning: human dignity based on fleeting prestige and authority is worthless in the face of divine judgment. Only submission to God offers true stability and true honor.

sens: Fortified city of the kingdom of Judah in the lowland region
Site of a battle against the Ethiopian Zerah
Site of a prophetic judgment against King Jehoshaphat
H4762G.detail:
1. Maréscha is a city in the territory of Judah, located in the lowlands (the Shephelah), mentioned alongside other cities like Keilah and Achzib (Joshua 15:44). Its name literally means "crest of a hill," evoking its location on a height. King Rehoboam fortified it to defend his kingdom (2 Chronicles 11:8).
2. It is near Maréscha that King Asa achieves a decisive victory against the army of Pharaoh Zerah: in the valley of Zephathah, at the gates of the city, the troops of Judah crush an Egyptian army of one million soldiers and three hundred chariots (2 Chronicles 14:8-9).
3. The city is also the starting point of a prophetic word from the prophet Eliezer against King Jehoshaphat: a resident of Maréscha, Eliezer announces that the Lord will break the king's ships because of his alliance with the king of Israel (2 Chronicles 20:37). The prophet Micah also mentions it as a place destined to witness the departure of Israel's glory (Micah 1:15).
H4762G.origine: The Hebrew name מָרֵשָׁה (Maréscha) comes from a root meaning "height" or "crest," which designates a geographical relief. The name aptly describes the nature of the site: a city established on a hill, overlooking the lowlands of Judah. This toponymy reveals how the ancient Hebrews named places according to their striking physical characteristics.
H4762G.emploi: Maréscha appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, always in significant historical or prophetic contexts. It first appears in the list of cities in the territory of Judah (Joshua 15:44), then in the list of cities fortified by Rehoboam (2 Chronicles 11:8). It becomes famous as the site of a major victory of King Asa against the Ethiopian invasion (2 Chronicles 14:8-9), a pivotal event in the history of Judah. It is then mentioned during the prophetic judgment pronounced against Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles 20:37) and figuratively by Micah (1:15) as a symbol of Judah's downfall. The city thus embodies the highs and lows of the kingdom's history: strategic fortification, site of victory, but also the starting point of prophetic warnings.

sens: Son of Laadah, of the tribe of Judah
Ancestor of the people associated with fine textile work
H4762H.detail:
1. Maréscha is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 4:21. He is the son of Laadah and belongs to the lineage of Judah.
2. The text presents him as an ancestor whose house or lineage is famous for working with fine linen (a delicate and precious fabric). His name is associated with families of artisans specialized in this delicate work.
H4762H.origine: The name Maréscha literally means "summit of a hill" or "crest" in Hebrew, evoking a height or elevation. In the Old Testament, this same name also designates a city in the lowlands of Judah, suggesting that the person may be linked to this place.
