The name reflects the topographical or social importance of the character in the context of the tribes of Judah.
H4762H.emploi: Maréscha appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:21, in a detailed genealogical list of the tribe of Judah. He is presented as an important link in the genealogical chain, as his name is followed by the mention of families famous for their work in textile crafts. His mention underscores that certain Jewish lineages were known and honored for their particular artisan skills.

sens: That which is placed at the head of the bed, particularly as support or pillow
The side of the head during rest or sleep
The area of the head of a person lying down
By extension, the place of honor or leadership
H4763.detail:
1. The chevet is primarily the object or place on which one rests their head while sleeping. Jacob uses a stone as a chevet during his night at Bethel (Genesis 28:11), and the next day he sets it up as a sacred monument, showing the importance of the place where his head rested.
2. The word then designates the area around the head of a sleeping person. Michal places a goat's hair at the chevet of the bed to deceive Saul's messengers (1 Samuel 19:13-16); David approaches the chevet of the sleeping Saul to take his spear (1 Samuel 26:7, 26:11), showing that it refers to the precise spot near the head.
3. The chevet can also simply refer to the head or the area of the head: it is a way of speaking where "what is at the chevet" means "what is at the head." 
4. Abstractly, the word carries the idea of dominance or place of power, since the head is the site of command and authority of the body.
H4763.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "head" (rosh). Merashot is a plural form of the word chevet, often indicating a position or place "at the head" (at the forefront). The basic image is that of the head, then that of what belongs to the head or what is placed near it. In Hebrew, the same group of words is used to express both physical command and authority.
H4763.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Bible, always in the singular in the French translation, specifically designating the object or place at the head of the bed where a person's head rests. All usages are narrative and concrete: Jacob lays his head on a stone (Genesis 28), Michal places an object at the chevet to simulate a sleeper (1 Samuel 19), and David approaches the chevet of the sleeping Saul to take his spear (1 Samuel 26). The word remains always material and spatial, designating the physical place near the head of a sleeper, never an abstract or metaphorical sense.
H4763.portee: The chevet reminds us that the most vulnerable moments of our lives — sleep, rest — are known to God. Jacob sees God at the moment he rests his head on a stone; David respects the sleeping Saul, recognizing that one does not touch the Lord's anointed. The chevet becomes the silent witness of our nights, of the rest that God gives us and of His watch during our weakness.

sens: Eldest daughter of King Saul
H4764.detail: Mérab is the eldest daughter of King Saul, mentioned for the first time in 1 Samuel 14:49 among the king's children. She is the sister of Jonathan, Abinadab, Malchishua, and Michal. Although Saul initially promised to give her to David as a wife (1 Samuel 18:17), this promise was not kept: Mérab was ultimately married to Adriel of Meholah (1 Samuel 18:19), and she had five children from this marriage.
H4764.origine: The name Mérab means "increase" or "multiplication" in Hebrew, an appropriate blessing for the daughter of a king. It comes from the Hebrew root רָבָה (rabah), which means "to increase" or "to become numerous." It is a name that evokes fertility and prosperity.
H4764.emploi: Mérab appears three times in the first book of Samuel, always in the accounts of the early reign of Saul. She is first named among the king's children (1 Samuel 14:49) to situate the royal family. She then becomes a political pawn: Saul promises her hand to David after his victory over the Philistines, but with the secret intention that David be killed in battle (1 Samuel 18:17). This promise is broken, and Mérab is given to Adriel of Meholah (1 Samuel 18:19), which frustrates Saul's plan to dispose of David through this marriage. Mérab then disappears from the biblical narrative, but Psalm 18:45 (titled "David's Prayer") and 2 Samuel 21:8 mention her children, confirming that this marriage had significant descendants.

sens: Fabric or cloth stretched over a bed or piece of furniture
Luxury garment or adornment
H4765.detail:
1. Fabric or cloth stretched over a bed or piece of furniture — The starting image is that of a fabric being spread out and unfolded. In Proverbs 7:16, the adulterous woman "adorns her bed with coverings": these are precious fabrics that cover the bed, often imported (here "of Egyptian linen") and therefore costly. The word designates the concrete object that adorns the furniture.
2. Luxury garment or adornment — The word extends to any type of fabric that decorates and protects. In Proverbs 31:22, the virtuous woman "makes herself coverings" and possesses fine garments: here, the word refers to pieces of adornment or precious fabrics that can be worn or accumulated as valuable possessions. The emphasis is on the quality and richness of the fabric.
H4765.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to spread out," "to unfold." It appears only twice in biblical Hebrew, making it a rather rare term and likely related to a context of luxury or wealth. The related verb evokes the action of unfolding a fabric, covering something with it.
H4765.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the book of Proverbs. In Proverbs 7:16, it is used in the context of seduction: the richly adorned coverings of the adulterous bed are a detail that enhances the atmosphere of luxury and temptation. In Proverbs 31:22, it characterizes the woman of value, who has the ability and resources to procure fine fabrics. In both cases, the word refers to a sign of wealth and social status, even though the ethical contexts differ greatly.
H4765.portee: These two uses remind the reader that material luxury and adornment seduce our senses, but only wisdom — embodied here by the woman of Proverbs 31 — makes good use of riches. The contrast between the two women invites reflection on true beauty and true value: that which comes from a wise and God-fearing life.

sens: extent, greatness of a whole
large quantity, profusion
growth, increase
power, domination that extends
H4766.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the extent, the greatness of a reality — the "government" in Isaiah 9:6 is the power of a kingdom that extends and grows: the Lord promises to continually increase this government of peace.
2. It also evokes an abundant quantity, a profusion: in Isaiah 33:23, the "immense spoil" is a mass, a heap of plunder taken from the enemy.
3. The word emphasizes the idea of growth, increase — that which grows, that which is added: there is always more, a continuous growth.
4. Used for power or domain, it expresses the domination that extends, the influence that grows without limit.
H4766.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to be many, to multiply." It is related to other Hebrew words expressing quantity, multiplication, and increase. It is a noun derived from a verbal form marking the action of becoming great, numerous, abundant. The starting image is that of accumulation, of continuous multiplication.
H4766.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Isaiah 9:6, it qualifies the "government" of the Messiah, whose rule will increase without end — a promise of peaceful and lasting dominion. In Isaiah 33:23, it describes an immense "spoil" taken from the defeated enemy. In both cases, it reinforces the idea of something that exceeds ordinary measure, that extends beyond all expectations. The royal and eschatological context of Isaiah marks its use.
H4766.portee: For the Bible reader, this word reminds us that the reign of the Messiah is not a limited or temporary power, but a government whose abundance and increase are without end. It invites contemplation of the magnificence of God's plan: the promise of a growing peace, of a justice that asserts itself forever. It is a word of hope rooted in the certainty that God's reign knows no limits or end.

sens: Important or considerable quantity
Abundance, profusion
That which fills or exceeds the usual measure
H4767.detail:
1. The word denotes a significant quantity, beyond what is usual or measured. In Ezekiel 23:32, the cup of judgment is large and contains "much" liquid, expressing its formidable abundance.
2. It evokes the idea of profusion or accumulation: not just "enough," but beyond, that which fills and overflows. It is the image of a cup so full that it intimidates the one who must drink it.
3. Figuratively, it can qualify any excess or superabundance, particularly in the expression of divine judgment: much misery, much suffering inflicted as punishment.
H4767.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of "much" or "abundance." It is related to other Hebrew terms of the same semantic family that describe multiplication, fullness, or that which overflows. This root reflects a concrete vision: that which is "much" is that which accumulates, fills space, and exceeds ordinary limits.
H4767.emploi: This word appears only once in the preserved Hebrew biblical text, in Ezekiel 23:32. It is used in a discourse of judgment from the Lord against Jerusalem, compared to an unfaithful woman. The cup meant to be drunk contains "much" — much drink (the divine judgment in symbolic form), much suffering and dishonor. The context emphasizes the excessive magnitude of the punishment: not a small cup, but a wide, deep cup filled with "much."
H4767.portee: This word reminds us that divine judgment, when it comes, is never partial or insufficient: it is full and abundant. For the reader, this can serve as a warning about the serious consequences of unfaithfulness to God, but also as assurance that His justice is complete and that nothing escapes His attention.

sens: Interest or profit charged on a loaned sum
Increase, growth of a quantity or number
Majority, larger part of a whole
Size, extent or importance of something
H4768.detail: 1. In matters of money or goods, it is the excessive interest that a lender demands beyond what he has loaned. The Law prohibits it among Israelites: "You shall not lend him your money at interest, nor lend him your food for profit" (Leviticus 25:37). It is an immoral gain derived from the misery of others. 2. It is also the increase or growth of something, its natural expansion. For a family or community, this means growth in number or power. 3. The majority or the larger part of a group: "the majority of them remained loyal to the house of Saul" (1 Chronicles 12:29). 4. Finally, it is the remarkable size or importance of something, its eminence. The queen of Sheba says of King Solomon: "the half of your greatness was not told me" (2 Chronicles 9:6).
H4768.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to be great, to be multiplied." It expresses the idea of a quantity that increases, of something that gains in size. The same family of words produces other terms concerning greatness and abundance.
H4768.emploi: This word appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in historical and legislative books. In a legal context (Leviticus), it designates the usurious interest that the Law prohibits. In historical passages (Samuel, Chronicles), it takes on the meaning of "majority" or "larger part," or that of "abstract greatness" such as royal wisdom. Its meaning changes according to the context: concrete when it concerns money, collective when counting people, abstract when qualifying a moral or intellectual quality.
H4768.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that the financial exploitation of the poor is contrary to God's justice. The Law protects the borrower by prohibiting usury, reflecting God's heart for the weak. It is also a call to uphold brotherly solidarity rather than greed.

sens: Place where animals (wild or domestic) lie down and stay
Habitat or shelter for a group of living beings
H4769.detail:
1. The word designates the place where beasts rest, sleep, and take refuge. It is their natural dwelling, their space of tranquility. In Ezekiel 25:5, God announces that the land of the Ammonites will become a "fold" for the sheep — a peaceful place where the flocks can settle and lie down without fear.
2. More broadly, it is a shelter, a refuge, a space to live and dwell. In Zephaniah 2:15, the proud city becomes a "den" for the beasts — a wild, desolate haven where animals make their home after ruin. The word always describes a space of habitation, but its meaning varies depending on what occupies it: peace of the flock or desolation inhabited by wild beasts.
H4769.origine: The Hebrew word מַרְבֵּץ comes from the root רבץ (rbts), which means "to lie down, to be lying, to rest." It evokes the image of physical rest: an animal that settles on the ground to rest. The word naturally designates the place where this rest occurs — the shelter, the place of lying down. The same root creates the image of rest and stable habitation.
H4769.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Bible, in two contexts of divine judgment. In Ezekiel 25:5, it paints the future of Rabbah and the land of the Ammonites transformed into peaceful pastures. In Zephaniah 2:15, it describes the fall of Nineveh, whose ruins become the den of wild beasts. In both cases, the word conveys a rupture: a human land becomes a space where animals settle, for good (flocks) or for desolation (wild beasts). It is a rare word, but rich in eschatological meaning.
H4769.portee: This word reminds us that true stable and lasting dwelling comes from God alone. Proud empires, like Nineveh, which seem so secure in their rest, collapse and make way for beasts. In contrast, the flock of God's people — the sheep — finds its peaceful shelter in the order established by the Lord. It is an invitation to recognize that our true rest relies only on God, not on our fortifications or human assurances.

sens: Stable or enclosure where animals are fattened
Animal intensively fed to make it fat
Fatty meat, tasty flesh
State of well-being or softness
H4770.detail:
1. The primary meaning is a place: a stable or an enclosure specialized in fattening livestock (Amos 6:4: "calves fattened"). It is a facility for feeding animals intensively so that they become fat and flavorful.
2. By extension, the word designates the animal itself that has been fattened: a fat and well-fed beast, ready to be eaten. In 1 Samuel 28:24, the woman kills "a fat calf" that she owned, the animal ready for culinary sacrifice.
3. The word can evoke the flesh itself, fatty and delicious: the "fattened calves" of Jeremiah 46:21 symbolize wealth and food abundance.
4. Figuratively, it represents ease, comfortable well-being, or softness: in Amos 6:4, the rich who "lie on ivory beds" and "eat the lambs of the flock" are associated with this fattening, as if they live in luxury and ease.
H4770.origine: The Hebrew word מַרְבֵּק (marbèq) comes from a root that means "to grow fat" or "to become fat." It literally describes the process and the place where animals are fattened by being abundantly fed. It is a concrete word, linked to the pastoral and agricultural life of Israel, where fattening livestock was a common practice to have tasty meat for feasts or important meals.
H4770.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the Hebrew Bible, always in a context of luxury or abundance. In 1 Samuel 28:24, it evokes a precious and well-fed animal. Jeremiah 46:21 uses it to portray the Egyptian soldiers as fat and soft beasts, unable to resist. Amos 6:4 denounces the rich of Israel who eat "fattened calves" with complete indifference to the misfortunes of the people: it is a symbol of insolent wealth. Finally, Malachi 4:2 offers a positive note, promising the faithful that they will "leap like calves from a stall," an image of joy and lightness.
H4770.portee: This word invites reflection on the contrast between earthly abundance and true spiritual wealth. In the prophet Amos, fattening becomes an image of sin: a carnal prosperity that blinds to justice and mercy. In contrast, in Malachi, the "calves" herald the freedom and joy promised to the righteous. The word reminds us that a life of excessive comfort can distance us from God, while the fear of His name brings a much deeper joy.

sens: State of calm and tranquility for the soul
Inner peace found by following God's righteous path
H4771.detail:
1. Rest here denotes a state of deep calm and tranquility of the soul, a peace that soothes inner turmoil. It is the opposite of agitation, worry, or troubled heart.
2. In the passage from Jeremiah, this rest is obtained by walking on the right path, that of the ancient just ways — that is, by listening to God's voice and obeying Him. It is a peace that comes not from an absence of effort, but from a life oriented according to divine will.
H4771.origine: The Hebrew word מַרְגּוֹעַ (margoa') comes from the root רגע (raga'), which means "to be calm, tranquil, at peace." This root evokes the image of something that becomes still after agitation. The word belongs to the family of biblical expressions designating the peace of heart and soul before God.
H4771.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 6:16. In this verse, the prophet reports the Lord's call to Israel: to seek the ancient paths and ask what the good way is to find rest for their souls. It is a rest promised to those who return to obedience and walk with God. The context shows that this rest is not a mere relaxation, but a deep peace linked to a right relationship with the Lord.
H4771.portee: For the believer, this verse teaches that true peace of the soul does not come from the world or its distractions, but from faithfulness to the word of God and returning to the "ancient paths" — the eternal truths of the Gospel. It is an invitation to seek rest not elsewhere, but in obedience and communion with God.

sens: Lower extremity of the leg, part of the body that touches the ground
Area at the bottom of a person lying down, where the feet are located
Lower part of a supernatural being or a vision
H4772.detail:
1. The foot is the part of the human body that rests on the ground. In Ruth 3:4, Ruth uncovers the feet of Boaz while he is sleeping to be near him and obtain his protection — an act of humility that respects the social order by approaching him by the feet rather than by the head.
2. In Israel, lying at someone's feet while they sleep expresses the expectation of protection or the desire to place oneself under their authority. Ruth 3:7-8 shows Boaz waking up and discovering a woman lying at his feet; it is a familiar but chaste act that seeks his help.
3. In celestial or divine beings, feet recall a human form. In Daniel 10:6, the angel of the vision has feet like polished bronze, a sign of his power and supernatural character.
H4772.origine: The Hebrew word marg'lot literally means "place of the feet." It comes from the root "raglès" (foot) and designates the space where the feet rest, hence its meaning of the lower part of the body. This term concretizes the idea of respectful proximity: being at someone's feet means placing oneself under their authority or protection.
H4772.emploi: This word appears only five times in the Hebrew Bible, all in the Book of Ruth and once in Daniel. In Ruth 3, the word is central to the scene of Goel-redemption where Ruth silently seeks Boaz by lying at his feet — a local custom of ritual request. In Daniel 10:6, the term describes the appearance of a celestial vision whose form resembles that of a man. The context changes according to the meaning: human and concrete in Ruth, visionary and supernatural in Daniel.
H4772.portee: For the Christian reader, this word illustrates how Scripture honors humility and trust: Ruth, defenseless, places her hope at the feet of Boaz, a type of redeemer. It teaches that seeking protection from a worthy man and praying in a position of humility are legitimate actions in the face of uncertainty.

sens: Projectile weapon used to throw stones
Instrument of punishment or divine judgment
H4773.detail:
1. A sling is a simple yet effective weapon: a strap or leather pouch attached to two cords, which is swung to project a stone far and hard. It is the weapon of a shepherd or a soldier without means; in Proverbs 26:8, the image is this: "to bind a stone in the sling" means to hold it in place to throw it, which is absurd if one misunderstands its use.
2. By extension, the sling becomes a biblical image of judgment or punishment: the one who holds it has the power to harm from a distance. This is why honoring or serving it without discernment (as one would do with a dangerous weapon entrusted to a fool) is contrary to wisdom.
H4773.origine: The Hebrew word מַרְגֵּמָה (marguemah) comes from the root רגם (ragam), which means "to throw stones" or "to stone." This root designates the action of throwing stones, either as punishment (stoning) or as a means of defense or war. The word naturally derives from this sense of projection to designate the instrument that makes it possible.
H4773.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Proverbs 26:8. It is used in a wisdom saying that compares the act of honoring a fool to the absurd act of fixing a stone in a sling: in both cases, power or importance is given to one who does not know how to use it wisely. The context is moral and pedagogical: it serves as a warning against foolishness.
H4773.portee: This image of the sling teaches the believer that entrusting authority or honor to one who lacks wisdom is not only vain but dangerous. It invites discernment regarding whom one grants credit and power, as bad hands can cause harm. It is a lesson in caution and discernment in human relationships.

sens: place where one rests
refuge, shelter
rest of the soul or heart
H4774.detail:
1. It is a physical, concrete place where someone comes to rest after fatigue or work. In Isaiah 28:12, it is the rest that God offers to the weary.
2. It is also an image of the refuge or shelter provided by peace with God — a place of safety and calm in the face of turmoil.
3. In a spiritual sense, it is the deep rest of the soul and heart, the inner peace that only God can give to one who ceases to struggle and worry.
H4774.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root רגע (ragaʿ), which means "to calm," "to soothe," "to remain quiet." The form מַרְגֵּעָה adds the prefix "מ" which transforms the idea of action into a concrete noun, a place or state. It evokes the image of agitation calming down, of a storm settling.
H4774.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 28:12. The prophet reports God's offer to Israel: a place of rest for the weary. But the people refuse to heed this word. The context shows that this rest is not only physical but spiritual — it is the rest that God grants to those who turn to Him and cease their own struggle.
H4774.portee: This word from Isaiah speaks to the heart of the Christian weary from life or from the efforts of the flesh. It reminds that God offers true rest — not idleness, but the peace of one who ceases to rely on their own strength and trusts in God. It is an invitation to enter into God's rest, a theme that the New Testament will revisit (see Hebrews 4).

sens: To refuse the authority of a king or leader and cease to obey him
To reject the authority of God and disobey His commandments
To refuse to follow the light or righteousness
H4775.detail:
1. To rebel is primarily a political act: a people or vassal refuses to remain subject to their king and shakes off the yoke of his authority. Kedorlaomer had subdued the Canaanite kings for twelve years; in the thirteenth year, these kings rebelled against him (Genesis 14:4). Hezekiah rebelled against the king of Assyria and refused to be his vassal (2 Kings 18:7). This rebellion is a voluntary act of rupture and insubordination.
2. The word takes on a serious spiritual significance when it designates rebellion against God. When Israel refuses the commandments of the Lord, it rebels — it is a turning away from its God, a breaking of the covenant. Ezekiel describes Israel as a rebellious people who have violated the ordinances of the Lord (Ezekiel 2:3). It is a sin that calls for divine wrath.
3. More rarely, the word designates those who are hostile to light or righteousness: Job speaks of those who are "enemies of the light," who refuse its ways and do not walk in its paths (Job 24:13). It is a voluntary turning away from the truth.
H4775.origine: The Hebrew verb מָרַד (marad) means properly "to rebel" or "to refuse authority." Its root expresses the idea of rupture and insubordination. In Aramaic, a similar form is found. This verb is encountered only in this very specific sense: it always designates an act of contested or refused authority, never a simple passive disobedience. It is a strong word that marks an active and deliberate rupture.
H4775.emploi: The verb מָרַד appears 23 times in the Old Testament, primarily to describe political rebellions against kings. It is found in 2 Kings (rebellions of Israel against Assyria) and in 2 Chronicles (rebellions against the kings of Judah). With God, it describes Israel's rebellion: the people have rebelled (Ezekiel 2:3, Daniel 9:5, Nehemiah 9:26). The rebellion can be collective (a people) or individual (a king). In all cases, it is a deliberate refusal of legitimate authority, whether human or divine, and it leads to serious consequences: the Lord's anger, judgment, or defeat.
H4775.portee: Understanding this word helps the Christian grasp the seriousness of disobedience to God. To rebel is not a simple oversight or weakness: it is an act of active hostility against established authority. This is why the Bible presents repentance as a return from rebellion: returning to God means ceasing to rebel against Him and recognizing His legitimacy. For the reader, this calls for humility and obedience.

sens: refusal to submit to established authority
open rebellion against a king or power
H4776.detail: 1. The word designates the categorical refusal to submit to one who has power: one does not obey him, one defies him. In Ezra 4:19, it is reported that Jerusalem "has engaged in sedition and rebellion" against the kings who governed it — that is, it refused their authority and rebelled against them. 2. More specifically, it is a concrete and visible rebellion: organized acts of disobedience, not just an inner thought or feeling. When Ezra describes the city as having "from ancient times" committed rebellions, he speaks of a historically attested conduct.
H4776.origine: The Aramaic word me.rad is the nominal form derived from the verb rad (rader in Aramaic), which means "to rebel, to revolt." It comes from the Hebrew מרד (méred), belonging to the same root. The Hebrew word also appears in the Bible to designate rebellion, notably against God Himself. The basic image is that of a rupture, a refusal to follow.
H4776.emploi: This Aramaic word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 4:19, in an official document of the Persian king that reports the accusations against Jerusalem. It is a historical inquiry where the antecedents of the city are sought to justify its prohibition of reconstruction. The "rebellion" mentioned is a concrete political fact: Jerusalem did indeed resist the kings who dominated it. It is an administrative and historical term, used neutrally by the document's author, without any explicit moral or religious connotation — it is simply the fact that the city refused obedience to its rulers.
H4776.portee: This word reminds us that disobedience to authority has concrete and lasting consequences: the rebellions of Jerusalem in the past have left traces in official records, even compromising its reconstruction. For the reader, it invites reflection on the weight of insubordination and how our acts of rebellion mark history and have long-term effects.

sens: Act of revolting against an authority, a law, an order
Refusal to submit to God and His commandments
H4777.detail:
1. Rebellion is the act of rising up against the one who commands, refusing their authority. In Joshua 22:22, it denotes a serious crime: the eastern Israelites swear that they have not committed rebellion against God by building an altar. It is the opposite of obedience.
2. Specifically, the word refers to rebellion against God Himself — the refusal to follow His laws and ways. It is a sin that separates the people from their Lord and provokes His judgment.
H4777.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to revolt" or "to rise against." It expresses the idea of someone who stands up, who rises against established authority. The same root appears in Aramaic (merád), showing how important this concept was in ancient biblical thought.
H4777.emploi: The word appears only once in biblical Hebrew, in the Old Testament, specifically in Joshua 22:22. It is used in a very solemn context: the eastern tribes of Israel defend themselves against having committed rebellion against the Lord. They publicly deny it before God and Israel, swearing that they have not renounced His covenant. This passage shows that rebellion is perceived as the supreme crime against God.
H4777.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that willfully turning away from God and His Word is a serious rebellion. It is not a mere failure or weakness, but an act of defiance against the one who has all rights over us. Meditating on this word invites us to examine our hearts: do we truly serve the Lord, or is there hidden rebellion within us?

sens: Man from the tribe of Judah living during the time of the divided monarchy
H4778.detail: Mered is a man from the tribe of Judah, mentioned twice in the genealogies of the book of Chronicles. He is the son of Ezra and has brothers Jether, Epher, and Jalon. He married at least twice: first to a woman who bore him several children (Miriam, Shammai, and Jischbach), and then to Bithiah, daughter of Pharaoh, who gave him other children (Jered, Heber, and Jekuthiel). His name means "rebellion" or "revolt" in Hebrew, although the Bible does not report any act of revolt concerning him.
H4778.origine: The name Mered comes from the Hebrew root "marad" which means "to revolt" or "to rebel." This same root appears elsewhere in the Bible to denote acts of rebellion or disobedience. It is unclear why this name was given to this man, but in Hebrew culture, names often carried a significance that reflected either the hopes of the parents or the circumstances of the birth.
H4778.emploi: Mered is mentioned only in the first book of Chronicles, in chapters 4:17 and 4:18, in the context of the genealogies of the tribe of Judah. These two verses list his children from two different marriages, highlighting the importance of his descendants in the genealogical history of Israel. The fact that his wife is a daughter of the Egyptian Pharaoh underscores the connections between the Jewish community and Egypt at that time.

sens: Who refuses to obey established authority
Who revolts against legitimate power
Who resists or opposes with insolence
H4779.detail: 1. The word describes one who refuses obedience to those who have the power to command — here, to a king or political authority. In Ezra 4:12, Jerusalem is called "rebellious" because its inhabitants refuse to acknowledge Persian rule and behave as an autonomous city. 2. More broadly, it refers to one who revolts or openly insurrects: the term carries the idea of active resistance, not just passive disobedience. In Ezra 4:15, it is said of Jerusalem that it "has been in rebellion since ancient times," showing that this rebellious character is a lasting and dangerous trait in the eyes of the authorities. 3. The adjective can also qualify one who openly defies, who opposes with effrontery — this is the very attitude of the rebel, who dares to contradict or resist those who have the right to command.
H4779.origine: The Hebrew word מָרַד (marad) comes from a root that expresses the idea of rising up against, refusing to be submissive. It is a political and social term: it does not speak of a mere contrary thought, but of an act of revolt. The related noun מְרִידָה (meridah) means "revolt" or "rebellion" — it is the action of the rebel. This vocabulary is common in empire narratives, where a city or people labeled as "rebellious" threatens the established order.
H4779.emploi: The word appears twice in the biblical text, both in Ezra 4, in a letter that adversaries of the Jews send to the Persian king to alert him against Jerusalem. The context is political: after the Babylonian exile, when the Jews begin to rebuild the Temple, their enemies denounce them to the king as a "rebellious city" (Ezra 4:12) and "harmful to kings" (Ezra 4:15). The term does not speak of an actual armed revolt, but of a disposition, a nature, a historical habit of resistance: the city has "the reputation" of being rebellious. It is a political accusation aimed at frightening the king by recalling past troubles.
H4779.portee: This word reminds the Christian that rebellion — the refusal to submit to authority — has serious political and social consequences. But it also invites discernment: a city can be called "rebellious" by those who do not want to recognize the rights of others to rebuild their lives. For the believer, the true issue is not just to obey or disobey, but to whom and why. It is an invitation to pray for wisdom and for God to protect His people in the face of adversaries' accusations.

sens: attitude of one who revolts against authority
rebellious, insubordinate character
H4780.detail:
1. Rebellion is the act or attitude of one who refuses obedience and revolts against the one who commands. It is the opposite of submission and docility. In 1 Samuel 20:30, Saul calls his son Jonathan a "rebel" because he refuses to comply with his royal will: Jonathan does not denounce David, the friend whom his father wants to kill, which constitutes a blatant disobedience in the eyes of the king.
2. The word also denotes the permanent character of rebellion, the habitual tendency of a person to resist authority. It is a disposition of the heart that expresses itself in insubordinate acts.
H4780.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of rising up against, refusing to submit. It is a name that designates the state or condition of one who is untamed, who will not bend. The context of 1 Samuel 20:30 shows that this rebellion is seen as a serious rupture of the bond of obedience between a son and a father, between a subject and a king.
H4780.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, specifically in 1 Samuel 20:30. Saul uses it to reproach Jonathan for his disobedience regarding David. This reproach reveals the dramatic tension of the narrative: Jonathan cannot obey Saul because his commitment to David takes precedence over filial obedience. It is a key moment where rebellion is not a trivial act, but the refusal to participate in the killing of an innocent.
H4780.portee: Rebellion is a serious theme in the Bible. This word reminds the believer that disobedience to established authority is a serious act that has consequences. Yet, Jonathan's case also teaches that sometimes obeying justice and friendship requires refusing an unjust authority. True fidelity is not blind obedience, but obedience enlightened by conscience and righteousness.

sens: supreme god of the Babylonians
H4781.detail: Merodach was the principal god worshiped by the Babylonians, particularly during the time of Nebuchadnezzar. He is the central deity of the Babylonian pantheon, associated with the city of Babylon itself and the power of the empire. The Bible mentions him when it announces the fall of Babylon and the destruction of its idols (Jeremiah 50:2).
H4781.origine: The Hebrew name מְרֹדָךְ literally means "your rebellion." It is the Hebrew transcription of a major Mesopotamian deity of Babylonian worship, known in Akkadian as Marduk. The Bible adopts this foreign name to refer to the god that the pagans worshiped.
H4781.emploi: Merodach appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 50:2, in a prophetic oracle announcing the destruction of Babylon. The prophet declares that the idols of Merodach will be overturned and shattered. This passage is set in a context of announcing God's judgment against Babylon and its false gods. The explicit mention of Merodach emphasizes that no Babylonian god, even the most powerful according to the Babylonians themselves, can stand against the true God.
H4781.portee: The Bible mentions Merodach to show that the gods of the pagan nations, even the most prestigious, are idols without true power in the face of the true God. This brief reference encourages the reader to recognize the vanity of all idolatrous worship and the certainty of divine judgment on the kingdoms that oppose Him.

sens: Jew who returned from exile with Zerubbabel
Cousin and adoptive father of Queen Esther
The one who delivered Israel from Haman's plot
Institutor of the Feast of Purim
H4782G.detail:
1. Mordecai is a Jew who was among the first exiles to return from Babylon with Zerubbabel, the leader of the return (Ezra 2:2 and Nehemiah 7:7). His name appears in these lists as one of the principal leaders of God's people during the restoration.
2. He was the cousin and adoptive father of Queen Esther, whom he raised after the death of her parents. This close relationship placed him in a position of influence at the court of King Ahasuerus.
3. In the account of the book of Esther (not provided in detail here but attested by the source), Mordecai was the principal agent of Israel's deliverance: he thwarted the plot of the minister Haman, who aimed for the complete extermination of the Jews scattered throughout the Persian empire.
4. Mordecai instituted the Feast of Purim in commemoration of this miraculous deliverance, a celebration still observed by the Jews.
H4782G.origine: The name literally means "little man" or possibly "worshiper of Mars" (Marduk in Akkadian). It bears the name of a Babylonian deity, a common reflection of the names given to exiles in foreign lands.
H4782G.emploi: Mordecai appears twice in the lists of return from exile (Ezra 2:2 and Nehemiah 7:7), always named among the leaders of the people who accompanied Zerubbabel. However, it is primarily the book of Esther that recounts his major role: faithful cousin, protector of young Esther, and architect of Israel's salvation in the face of threats from Persian power. His example shows how God can act discreetly through individuals placed in strategic positions.
H4782G.portee: The story of Mordecai teaches that God watches over His people even in exile and dispersion, placing His servants in key positions through which He can intervene. It also reminds us that faithfulness to one's own (he raised Esther with dedication) and courage in the face of injustice reflect divine providence.

sens: Jew from the tribe of Benjamin living in Susa during the exile and return
Cousin and adoptive father of Queen Esther
The one who discovered and denounced the plot against the king
Liberator of the Jews from the danger planned by Haman
Institutor of the Feast of Purim
Man promoted to great honors in the kingdom
H4782H.detail:
1. Mordecai is a Jew from the tribe of Benjamin, introduced at the beginning of the book of Esther as a man living in Susa, the capital of the Persian kingdom. He first appears as an ordinary character, simply named in chapter 2 (Esther 2:5).

2. He becomes the guardian and adoptive father of Esther after the death of her parents. It is in this discreet role that he raises her and watches over her, showing constant affection while remaining in the background (Esther 2:11).

3. Mordecai demonstrates vigilance by discovering a plot to assassinate King Ahasuerus and informing Queen Esther, who reports it to the king in his name (Esther 2:22).

4. When the prime minister Haman, offended by Mordecai's refusal to bow down, plots to annihilate all the Jews, it is Mordecai who, through divine providence and Esther's action, becomes the instrument of their deliverance (Esther 3:6 and following).

5. After this deliverance, Mordecai and Esther institute the Feast of Purim to commemorate the salvation (Esther 9:29-31).

6. His status gradually rises until he is honored by the king and established in great power in the kingdom (Esther 6:11, Esther 8:9).
H4782H.origine: The name Mordecai comes from the Hebrew מׇרְדֳּכַי (Mardekhai). It probably derives from Persian, with a possible meaning of "little man" or "worshiper of Mars" according to ancient traditions. This name reflects the cosmopolitan context of the Persian court, where a Jew bears a name of foreign origin while remaining faithful to his identity and his people. The character belongs to the period of exile and return of Israel, a time when the dispersed Jews had to navigate between their faith and their life in foreign kingdoms.
H4782H.emploi: Mordecai is the central character of the book of Esther, mentioned about 50 times in this historical book. He first appears as an ordinary Jew in Susa (Esther 2:5), then as Esther's guardian (Esther 2:7, 2:10, 2:11). He distinguishes himself by denouncing a plot against the king (Esther 2:21, 2:22), which puts him in contrast with Prime Minister Haman, who hates him and seeks his destruction (Esther 3:2-6). At the heart of the narrative, Mordecai refuses to bow down before Haman, a refusal that shows his fidelity to his religious principles in the face of Persian protocol (Esther 3:2-4). After Haman's downfall and the overturning of his plans through Esther's intervention, Mordecai moves from a position of humiliation to one of honor and authority (Esther 6:11, Esther 8:2, Esther 8:9). He then becomes a man of power who writes in the king's name to protect the Jews (Esther 8:9, Esther 9:3).
H4782H.portee: Mordecai's journey illustrates how a man faithful to his religious convictions, even in adversity and exile, can become an instrument of divine providence for the deliverance of his people. His story teaches that discretion, vigilance, and personal integrity have value, even when they are not immediately recognized. It also shows that God acts to protect His people, sometimes in hidden ways and through seemingly ordinary circumstances, without spectacular miracles.

sens: Action of relentlessly pursuing someone
Oppression exercised against someone mercilessly
Punishment that befalls a persecutor
H4783.detail:
1. The word literally denotes the action of pursuing someone without stopping, like a hunter tracking its prey. In Isaiah 14:6, the king of Babylon who struck the peoples "with relentless blows" is himself "pursued without mercy": it is the same violence, the same relentlessness, that returns to him.
2. By extension, it refers to any continuous and merciless oppression inflicted on someone. The word evokes the idea of a person who cannot find rest, always hunted or crushed.
3. In the prophetic context, persecution can also be understood as divine punishment: the one who has persecuted others suffers in turn a merciless persecution, reflecting God's justice.
H4783.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root "rdp" which means "to pursue" or "to track." This root evokes the image of relentless pursuit, like that of a hunter after its prey. Other words from the same family express the idea of hunting, of pursuing insistently. It is a concrete word that has taken on a moral and spiritual meaning: to pursue someone is to persecute them.
H4783.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 14:6, in an oracle against the king of Babylon. The prophet announces that the one who crushed the peoples "with relentless blows" will in turn be "pursued without mercy." This unique usage highlights retributive justice: the persecutor becomes persecuted in turn. The context is a divine judgment pronounced against a tyrant.
H4783.portee: This word reminds the reader that persecution is not a permanent power: the one who oppresses the weak does not escape God's justice. Isaiah announces that tyrants will be caught up in punishment, and that God protects His oppressed people. It is a word of comfort for the victims.

sens: Refuse to obey, stand against authority
Show insubordination, disobedience towards someone
Exhibit bitterness, resentment
Be obstinate, rebellious in one's plans
H4784.detail:
1. To rebel primarily means to categorically refuse to obey an order or authority. Moses calls the Israelites "rebels" when they refuse to follow him (Numbers 20:10), because they no longer recognize his authority. It is the radical refusal of submission.

2. The word then describes an attitude of persistent insubordination: to be rebellious is to show that one does not want to accept a command or direction. The Israelites have been "rebellious against the Lord since the Lord knows them" (Deuteronomy 9:24) — a rebellion that spans time and defines a character.

3. The word can also express an inner bitterness, a resentment that drives one to revolt. When the people have "bitterness in their soul" in 1 Samuel 30:6, it is a feeling of resentment that makes them hostile, close to revolting.

4. Finally, rebellion can be a stubborn obstinacy: to rebel is to persist in plans contrary to what is requested. The Israelites "showed themselves rebellious in their plans" (Psalms 106:43), refusing to change course despite God's deliverances.
H4784.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of standing up, opposing head-on. The basic image is that of a person standing face to face with someone and refusing to advance, refusing to obey. The noun "bitterness" (מָרוּת, marout) comes from the same family: that which is bitter in taste. The Bible thus associates rebellion with a feeling of bitterness, as if the rebellious heart were filled with something unpleasant, unacceptable.
H4784.emploi: The verb appears 44 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical books and the Psalms. It primarily describes Israel's rebellion against God and His commandments, particularly in the wilderness (Numbers, Deuteronomy). It is also applied to disobedient children towards their parents (Deuteronomy 21:18), to peoples rebelling against kings (1 Kings 13:21), or to behaviors of general insubordination. The prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel) use it abundantly to denounce Israel's refusal to listen to the divine Word. The meaning remains constant: a voluntary opposition to legitimate authority.
H4784.portee: Understanding the rebellion described by this word helps the Christian recognize their own attitude towards God. It is not just an isolated sin; it is a posture of the heart that stands against divine authority. The word invites humility and obedience: it is the opposite of rebellion to bow before God and receive His commandments. For one who struggles against disobedience, meditating on the weight of this word in Scripture can lead them back to joyful submission.

sens: Source of bitter water in the Sinai Peninsula
Stop on the journey of the Israelites after crossing the Red Sea
H4785.detail:
1. Mara is a source of bitter water discovered by the Israelites three days after crossing the Red Sea (Exodus 15:23). The name of the place comes precisely from the bitterness of the water: "they could not drink the water of Mara because it was bitter. Therefore, the place was called Mara."
2. It is a campsite on the route through the Sinai desert, located between the crossing of the Red Sea and the oasis of Elim with its twelve springs and seventy palm trees (Numbers 33:8-9). Mara marks a known stop on the journey of the Israelites after their liberation from Egypt.
H4785.origine: The Hebrew name מָרָה (Mara) literally means "bitter" or "bitterness." It comes from the root מרר (marèr) which expresses what is bitter in taste or bitter to the soul. This descriptive name was given to the place because the water found there was unfit for drinking.
H4785.emploi: Mara appears three times in the Bible, all in the account of the Exodus. In Exodus 15:23, it is the first well encountered after crossing the Red Sea: the water there is bitter, causing tension among the people of Israel in the desert. In Numbers 33:8-9, Mara is recorded as an official stop on the route in the desert, between the starting point and the oasis of Elim. In these three mentions, Mara remains essentially the same place: a source of water unfit for consumption, a challenge in the journey through the desert.
H4785.portee: Mara teaches the believer that the spiritual desert holds trials where expected resources are lacking. It is a moment when faith must persevere while awaiting God's help, who will transform this bitter water (according to Exodus 15:25, Moses will cry out to the Lord and the water will become sweet). This stop reminds us that God's promises are fulfilled gradually, through difficulties.

sens: Bitter taste, unpleasant in the mouth
Feeling of sorrow, disappointment, or deep regret
H4786.detail: 1. Bitterness is primarily a physical sensation: an unpleasant or even repulsive taste. But in the Bible, the word mainly describes a moral and emotional bitterness. 2. It is the pain that fills the heart when one suffers, when one is hurt or disappointed. In the only biblical usage of the word, the wives of Isaac brought "bitterness" to his heart and that of Rebekah—not by their taste, but by their behavior and ideas, which caused deep sorrow to the parents (Genesis 26:35).
H4786.origine: The Hebrew word מֹרָה comes from the root that evokes what is bitter, harsh to the palate. In Hebrew, "bitterness" refers to both taste and feeling: the two are linked, as a bitter flavor is repulsive, unpleasant, just as pain is difficult to bear. This image of an unfortunate taste expresses the idea of an emotion that "does not pass," that remains stuck in the throat.
H4786.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 26:35. Isaac and Rebekah were deeply pained— their hearts were "bitter"—because of the women their sons had married, particularly Esau. These wives were Hittites and did not share the faith of the patriarchs. The bitterness was thus that of parents who saw their children straying from God's will. This context shows that biblical bitterness arises from the conflict between what one hopes for and the painful reality.
H4786.portee: This word reminds us that the choices of our children or loved ones can deeply wound us. But it also invites us to seek the true source of this bitterness: is it a legitimate concern for faith and the future, or a bitterness that fills our hearts and distances us from God? The text suggests that this pain was justified, but that it should be entrusted to the Lord rather than allowed to become a lasting wound.

sens: Bitter, acrid taste, unpleasant to the palate
Deep pain, intimate sorrow that only the one who feels it truly knows
H4787.detail:
1. In the literal sense, bitterness is the acrid and unpleasant taste one experiences in the mouth—opposed to sweetness. It is characteristic of certain plants or substances.
2. In a figurative sense, bitterness refers to the deep and personal pain of the heart. In Proverbs 14:10, "the heart knows its own sorrows": only the one who truly suffers can measure their own pain; no outsider can share their inner joy or affliction. It is a striking image of existential loneliness in the face of pain.
H4787.origine: The Hebrew word מׇרָּה (morah) comes from the root מרר (marrar), "to be bitter," which primarily expresses a physical sensation of unpleasant taste. This root evokes the idea of hardness, acridity—something that "stings" or "burns" the mouth. Related terms include מֵרִי (merî) and terms related to rebellion or opposition (as the bitter "resists" the palate). Bitterness naturally becomes a biblical image of moral suffering.
H4787.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 14:10. It refers to the hidden pain of the heart—not a general bitterness or hostility towards others, but the intimate and incommunicable trial that each person bears alone. This sapiential context shows that bitterness is primarily an inner reality, a personal wound that no one has the right to judge from the outside.
H4787.portee: This word invites the reader to silent compassion: behind the face of those around you may lie a deep bitterness that you do not suspect. The Bible thus reminds us of our natural inability to truly know the sorrows of others—and therefore our need for gentleness, patience, and kindness towards those who suffer without crying out.

sens: State of destitution and wandering
Moral and physical distress
Condition of one who is without refuge
H4788.detail:
1. The word designates the state of one who wanders aimlessly and without shelter, lacking the essentials. In Isaiah 58:7, it describes the "homeless unfortunate" that the believer must welcome—people driven from their homes, without a place to stay, forced to wander.
2. It also expresses deep distress, the affliction of the soul in the face of trials. In Lamentations 1:7, Jerusalem remembers its past splendor "in the days of its distress and misery," when it had fallen under the oppressor—this is an existential misery, not just material.
3. In Lamentations 3:19, the poet groans, "when I think of my affliction and my misery": he evokes the weight of misfortune that crushes the mind, the bitterness of living in affliction.
H4788.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes wandering movement, the idea of straying without direction. It is linked to the image of one who wanders, who has no fixed home—hence its sense of vagabondage and destitution. It is a concrete word at first (physical wandering) that has taken on a broader significance (moral affliction).
H4788.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, only in the books of Lamentations and Isaiah, texts that speak of suffering and ruin. In Isaiah 58:7, it refers to material and social misery—the homeless that justice calls to help. In Lamentations 1:7 and 3:19, the word fits into the prophetic theme of the pain of Jerusalem and the people in exile: misery becomes the lot of one who has lost their land, their temple, their stability. It is always a misery that cries out for help, that demands compassion and intervention.
H4788.portee: This word awakens the Christian on two points. First, it reminds them of their duty to see and relieve the misery of others—that of wanderers, the homeless, those wounded by life. Secondly, it gives a name to inner suffering: even when the body is well, the soul can be in misery, in distress. It is an invitation to recognize misery in its two forms and to be touched by it.

sens: Location in northern Palestine, mentioned only once in the Bible
H4789.detail: Meroz is a city or village located in northern Palestine. It appears only in the Song of Deborah (Judges 5:23), where the angel of the Lord curses its inhabitants because they did not participate in the battle against Sisera, the Canaanite general, while other Israelite peoples rose up to defend the Lord.
H4789.origine: The name Meroz literally means "refuge" in Hebrew, suggesting a place of protection or shelter. It is an ancient Palestinian geographical name whose exact equivalent is not known in extrabiblical sources.
H4789.emploi: Meroz appears only once in the entire Bible, in Judges 5:23. This passage is the Song of Deborah, composed shortly after the victory of the Israelites over Sisera and the Canaanite army (around the 12th century B.C.). The context shows that Meroz was an Israelite community capable of participating in the defense of the people but chose not to do so, thus deserving divine curse for its inaction in the face of God's call.
H4789.portee: This passage teaches that inaction and refusal to stand with God in critical moments carry moral guilt: it is not only evil acts that are condemned, but also the absence of courage and commitment when faith and justice demand it. Meroz becomes the biblical symbol of spiritual cowardice.

sens: That has been flattened, broken, or damaged by pressure or impact
That has damaged or defective testicles
H4790.detail:
1. The word describes something that is crushed, broken, or bruised by pressure. The image is that of an object being crushed under a weight, losing its shape or integrity. In Leviticus 21:20, it qualifies a physical defect that, like the others listed in this passage (hunchbacked, blemished, scabby), rendered a man unfit to serve as a priest.
2. More specifically, the word applies to crushed or damaged testicles, meaning rendered defective by injury or malformation. This is precisely the meaning of the passage in Leviticus 21:20, where this defect appears in a list of physical conditions that excluded the candidate from priestly service.
H4790.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root רוח (roach), which expresses the idea of crushing, grinding, or damaging by compression. This root evokes a vigorous action that destroys the integrity or shape of something. The word is used in contexts where defects or physical damages are depicted.
H4790.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Leviticus 21:20. It is part of a list of physical defects enumerated by God to Moses, which prohibited a man of Aaron's descendants from approaching the altar to perform priestly service. This list aimed to preserve the holiness of the priestly function and to maintain strict ritual purity in worship. The context shows that crushed is understood here literally as a visible and permanent bodily damage.
H4790.portee: This passage shows how the Old Testament viewed certain physical defects as incompatible with priestly service according to the Mosaic covenant. For today's believer, it serves as a reminder that direct access to God, once reserved for 'perfect' priests, is now open to all through Jesus Christ, our Great High Priest, who has accomplished the sacrificial service once for all. This progression reveals God's grace that transcends the ritual limitations of the old law.

sens: Vertical dimension of a place or an elevated thing
Place located above, summit or dominant position
Elevation, dignity, or high rank
Arrogance, pride, or haughty attitude
H4791.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the vertical measurement of a place — what is above in relation to what is below. In Judges 5:18, it speaks of the 'heights of the fields,' the elevated areas of the terrain. This is a concrete and geographical fact.
2. It also evokes the place itself that is elevated: a summit, a refuge located above. Isaiah 33:16 speaks of 'high places' where the one whom God protects dwells, like natural fortresses. It is a dominant and fortified space.
3. By extension, the word applies to the position, authority, or dignity of a person. Job 5:11 recounts how God 'raises' the humble (brings them out of lowliness to place them high). It conveys the idea of promotion, a place of honor.
4. Finally, it describes arrogance or pride — an attitude where one places oneself 'high' above others. Psalms 75:6 warns: 'Do not lift your head so high, do not speak with such arrogance!' The word then becomes a critique of pretension and contempt.
H4791.origine: This word comes from a root meaning 'to be high, to rise.' It is related to the image of ascent and domination. The family of the word includes forms that describe what is exalted, what rises, or what reigns. It is a concrete word at first — physical geography — which gradually enriches with a moral and spiritual meaning: height becomes the emblem of power, divine authority, and also the sin of pride.
H4791.emploi: The word appears 52 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Psalms, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. It first describes earthly realities: the heights of terrain (Judges 5:18), the elevated places where one takes refuge (Isaiah 33:16, 37:24). But very often, it applies to God: the Psalms place Him 'on high' (Psalms 93:4, 102:20), in His heavenly dwelling (Jeremiah 25:30), far from human sight. It expresses His transcendence and unmatched authority. The word can also describe moral elevation — how God lifts the righteous and brings down the wicked. Finally, it critiques the arrogance of humans who consider themselves 'high': Psalms 75:6 and Isaiah 26:5 illustrate this.
H4791.portee: This word opens the believer's eyes to two essential realities. First, it reminds us that God alone dwells 'on high,' out of reach and master of all. It is an invitation to humility: we are not 'high.' Secondly, it warns against pride — this sin of 'lifting' oneself, placing oneself above others. The height we should seek is not our own, but that of God, and wisdom is to submit to it.

sens: lake in northern Canaan
site of defeat of Canaanite kings against Joshua
H4792.detail: 1. Merom is a lake located in northern Canaan, formed by the Jordan River, about 16 kilometers north of the Sea of Galilee. It is an important water point in the region. 2. Merom is best known as the site of a decisive battle: it is where Joshua achieved a stunning victory against a confederation of Canaanite kings led by Jabin. These kings had gathered there to fight Israel (Joshua 11:5), but Joshua attacked them by surprise with his army and crushed their coalition (Joshua 11:7).
H4792.origine: The name Merom means 'high place' in Hebrew, likely referring to the lake's position in the Upper Jordan Valley. It is a geographical name that specifically designates this body of water in northern Canaan.
H4792.emploi: Merom appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the book of Joshua, chapter 11. The passage describes the moment when the northern Canaanite kings gather by the waters of Merom to confront Israel (Joshua 11:5), and immediately afterward, the sudden arrival of Joshua with his army who crushes this coalition (Joshua 11:7). These two verses recount a single military campaign that allowed Joshua to conquer northern Canaan.
H4792.portee: This victory at Merom demonstrates the power of God granted to Israel: a large and well-equipped army of Canaanite kings was defeated by the tactics and faith of Joshua. It is a biblical example of how God gives victory to His people when they act with courage and obedience.

sens: Rapid movement of a person or animal that is running
Action of participating in a speed competition
Undertaking or action carried out with zeal and speed
Result or outcome of an action that one pursues
H4793.detail:
1. In a concrete sense, the race is the act of running, of moving quickly. It is the physical action of someone who accelerates their pace to go fast, like a runner who takes off.
2. It is also the competition or speed trial where several competitors compete to arrive first: the one who runs the fastest wins the race.
3. In a figurative sense, the race refers to any endeavor carried out with effort and determination, anything that one actively pursues. In Ecclesiastes 9:11, the Preacher observes that "the race is not to the swift," meaning that the success of an endeavor, an action pursued with zeal, does not depend solely on who runs the fastest or works the hardest.
4. By extension, the race represents the outcome or result of what one undertakes, often beyond our control: it is what happens at the end of our efforts.
H4793.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root רוץ (routz) which means "to run." This root describes rapid movement, the action of propelling oneself forward. It is found throughout the Bible to speak of someone who runs, rushes, or pursues an action with zeal. The noun מֵרוֹץ (merotts) is its nominal derivative: it is the name given to the action of running, to the race itself.
H4793.emploi: This word appears only once in the Old Testament: in Ecclesiastes 9:11. The Preacher uses it to say that "the race is not to the swift." In this context, the word takes on a broader meaning than simple speed competition: it signifies the effort one expends to achieve a goal, the endeavor one pursues. The author teaches that speed, agility, or talent are not enough to guarantee success; other factors, time and circumstances, play a decisive role. This passage uses the race as an image of all human action: just as the fastest does not always win the race, the most capable does not always succeed in their endeavors.
H4793.portee: This passage invites the believer to recognize that our efforts, our abilities, and our zeal do not always control the final outcome. It calls us to place our trust not in ourselves, but in God, who governs time and circumstances. It is an invitation to humility and dependence on the Lord, rather than the pride of believing that our mere effort will guarantee victory.

sens: The act of running, the way one moves quickly
The trajectory or path traveled while running
In a figurative sense, the direction or course of life, the orientation of an existence
H4794.detail: 1. The word primarily refers to the act of running, the way of moving quickly. In 2 Samuel 18:27, the watchman observes the "manner of running" of the approaching messenger — his characteristic gait that allows him to be identified from afar. It is the concrete image of the runner in action. 2. It can also mean the path or distance covered during a race. It is the "route" taken by the one who runs, the path they follow at high speed. 3. In a figurative sense, it is the "race" or the "course" of life, meaning the direction in which one rushes, the moral orientation of one's existence. In Jeremiah 8:6, the people "return to their course" towards evil like a horse rushing into battle — they return to their bad habits with impetuosity. In Jeremiah 23:10, the wicked "run to evil": they energetically launch themselves into sin, unable to stop.
H4794.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to run" or "to rush." It primarily evokes the rapid and impetuous movement of the body. The basic image is that of the runner taking off, of accelerated movement. Over time, this concrete word has taken on a moral and figurative sense: "to run" also means to direct oneself, to orient oneself, and even to "engage foolishly" in a path. This is why "the course of life" can be good (Ahimelech bringing good news) or bad (the people rushing towards evil).
H4794.emploi: This word appears three times in the Bible in Hebrew. In 2 Samuel 18:27, it describes the manner of running of a messenger — a concrete and physical observation. In the two passages from Jeremiah (8:6 and 23:10), its use becomes figurative: "returning to their course" and "running to evil" express voluntary orientation, impetuous engagement in a path. The text of Jeremiah 8:6 even compares this "race" to the gallop of a battle horse, emphasizing the uncontrolled energy and impossibility of stopping. Thus, the word shifts from the concrete (the way of running) to the moral (the direction taken by existence or the heart).
H4794.portee: This word teaches us that our "race" — our life path — is not neutral: it has a moral direction. Are we running towards God, like Ahimelech who runs with good news? Or are we being swept away, like the people of Jeremiah, towards evil and iniquity? The image of the race invites us to examine the deep orientation of our choices and habits. It also reminds us that changing direction requires awareness and will.

sens: Care of the body through rubbing, anointing, and perfumes
Cosmetic and hygienic preparation of a woman
H4795.detail:
1. The Hebrew word marouq literally refers to the action of rubbing or scraping the skin. In Esther 2:12, it refers to the body care that the young women destined for the harem of King Ahasuerus received for twelve months: six months of anointing with myrrh oil, followed by six months of treatments with spices and perfumes. It is a complete treatment to soften, perfume, and beautify the skin.
2. By extension, this word evokes all the cosmetic and hygienic preparation of a woman, a set of practices to clean, care for, and adorn the body before an important occasion. In this royal context, the toilet was an elaborate protocol of long duration, not a simple wash.
H4795.origine: The Hebrew word marouq comes from the root "maraq," which fundamentally means "to rub" or "to scrape." This root evokes the physical gesture of cleaning or polishing a surface by rubbing it. It refers to the concrete image of the work of hands on the skin to prepare, clean, and beautify it.
H4795.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Esther 2:12. It describes the routine of care imposed on the young women of the Persian royal harem before their presentation to King Ahasuerus. The term emphasizes the duration (twelve months) and the richness of the products used (myrrh, spices, perfumes), reflecting the luxury and meticulous care of the royal court of the time. It is a technical word, very specific to the context of harem life.
H4795.portee: This passage shows us how ancient cultures placed great importance on physical beauty and body care, particularly in royal courts. For the Christian reader, this may invite reflection on the distinction between reasonable care of the body and excessive pursuit of appearance, a theme that other biblical passages address more clearly (such as 1 Peter 3:3).

sens: city in the low region of Judah
H4796.detail: Maroth is a city located in the Shephelah, the region of low hills that extends between the coast and the mountains of Judah. Its Hebrew name means "bitterness" or "bitter," possibly evoking a source or a well with bitter waters near the site. It is mentioned only once in Micah 1:12, where the prophet lists the cities of Judah that will face divine judgment.
H4796.origine: The name Maroth comes from a Hebrew root meaning "bitter." This place name reflects a geographical or natural characteristic of the site, likely related to its waters.
H4796.emploi: Maroth is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Micah 1:12. The prophet Micah lists the cities of Judah and Benjamin that will experience invasion and judgment; Maroth is among them, associated with other localities like Gath and Akzib. The context is that of the enemy's advance on Judean territory and the desolation that results from it.

sens: Cry raised during a celebration or feast
Exclamation expressing collective exultation and joy
H4797.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the shout made during a celebration or festivity — a loud exclamation of joy. In Amos 6:7, it refers to the "shouts of joy of those indulgent ones": the wealthy and carefree people shout with delight during their feasts and entertainments.
2. More broadly, it represents the collective voice of exultation, the audible expression of pleasure's intoxication. The term evokes not only the feeling of joy but its loud bursting forth, the clamor of people given to rejoicing. This is why such joy, based solely on carnal pleasures, is, in the prophetic context of Amos, fragile and destined to disappear.
H4797.origine: The word comes from a root that expresses the idea of crying out or shouting. It is related to other Hebrew words denoting cries — whether of joy, distress, or lamentation. The context determines whether it is a joyful cry or a cry of mourning: here, it is clearly a festive shout.
H4797.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Amos 6:7. The prophet Amos uses it to denounce the wealthy of Samaria who indulge in luxury and carelessness: they shout with joy without fear of God, feasting indifferently amid the injustices of the world. This superficial and carnal shout of joy is presented as one of the things God will cause to disappear during judgment.
H4797.portee: This word reminds us that there is a difference between true joy, rooted in God, and loud exultation based solely on material pleasures and moral indifference. The joy of the carefree is fragile; only joy in God endures.

sens: Cry of funeral lamentation
Gathering of mourners around a dead person
Place or house where the dead are mourned
State of collective sorrow and affliction
H4798.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a cry, a lamentation made by mourners during funerals. It is a characteristic sound of the mourning ritual in ancient Israel: a cry that expresses the sorrow of loss and was loudly emitted by women and close relatives of the deceased (Jeremiah 16:5, where God forbids the prophet from entering a house of mourning).
2. The word can also refer to the assembly itself, the gathering of mourners who come together around the dead or their family to share in the mourning and lament together.
3. By extension, it evokes the house or place where this gathering occurs — the house of mourning — where the family of the deceased receives condolences and where the cry of lamentation resounds. This is precisely what Jeremiah is forbidden to visit: a mourning household.
4. More broadly, it represents the collective emotional state: the shared sorrow, the affliction of the people when they lose someone dear or when the Lord withdraws His favor from Israel.
H4798.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes a cry, a voice that rises. It is related to verbs meaning to cry out, to proclaim, or to announce. The basic image is thus that of a voice resounding — in this case, the plaintive cry of the mourners. The word captures the audible and public nature of mourning in biblical times: it was not a silent and private affliction, but a loud and collective demonstration of sorrow.
H4798.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jeremiah 16:5. It is used in the context of a prohibition: the Lord commands the prophet Jeremiah not to enter a house of mourning to share in the sorrow with the mourners. This prohibition is a symbolic sign that divine judgment is approaching — there will soon be no more private mourning, but national devastation. The context shows that marzéach refers both to the act of lamenting, the assembly of mourners, and the place where the mourners gather.
H4798.portee: For the Christian, this verse from Jeremiah reminds us that Israel had its mourning rites and customs, and that the Lord was ready to remove them as judgment. This underscores that God takes seriously the cry of the people and the sorrow of humans — and that He can either forbid or restore them according to His will. It is also an invitation to meditate on what it truly means to weep with those who weep: mourning is not just a personal emotion, but an act of communion and solidarity that God can consecrate or suspend.

sens: To apply a substance on a surface by lightly rubbing
To spread, cover by rubbing
H4799.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of taking a substance (here a paste or a poultice of figs) and rubbing or applying it directly to a wound or area of the body to heal it. It is a medical or healing gesture: one "spreads" the figs on Hezekiah's ulcer (Isaiah 38:21) to heal him, just as one would apply a balm or remedy by rubbing it on the sick skin.
2. More broadly, the word evokes the action of spreading, covering a surface by rubbing or spreading a material: it is the concrete gesture of taking something in hand and pressing it, spreading it over what one wants to heal or cover.
H4799.origine: The Hebrew verb מָרַח (marach) belongs to a small family of words that express rubbing or application by friction. The root evokes the physical idea of passing something over a surface by applying slight pressure. It is not a common verb in the Bible: it appears only once, and it describes a very specific gesture from ancient medical practice.
H4799.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 38:21. It occurs in the context of the miracle of Hezekiah's healing: the prophet Isaiah commands that figs be brought and spread (marach) on the king's ulcer so that he may live. It is a concrete term used for a simple and direct therapeutic gesture. Its biblical context associates it with the medical practices of the ancient world: figs, which have soothing properties, are applied directly to the wound.
H4799.portee: This verb reminds us that God uses ordinary means and natural remedies to heal His people. Hezekiah's healing unites prayer, the prophet's intervention, and the use of a simple and accessible treatment. This humble gesture of spreading a remedy on a wound indicates that God often acts through ordinary means and that faith does not exclude the use of medicine and common sense.
